#9791. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

What will you build? Share your scene and results in the Hugging Face comments, including the assets and Isaac Sim version you used.

#9790. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

#9789. The four days no email went out

Posted on Nov 16 • Originally published at jonasnguyen.com

On October 11, the errors page in Clienzo's admin showed something new: "Platform email failed", twice.

Clienzo sends email through Brevo. Brevo has a security setting called Authorised IPs: only requests from listed IP addresses are accepted. It was switched on.

Clienzo's servers run on Google Cloud Run, which sends outgoing traffic from addresses that are not fixed. Once requests started coming from an address that was not on the list, Brevo rejected them with a 401 that mentioned an "unrecognised IP address".

Looking back through the logs, the last successful email was a welcome email on October 6. From October 7 to October 11, every send failed — 175 of them. Most were notifications about spam hitting the website's contact form, but in between were billing and support emails that never arrived.

Nothing crashed. The app kept working; sending email is a side effect of other actions, and a failed side effect does not stop the main one. A customer who does not receive an email usually does not write in to say so. They just assume you never sent it.

The fix was a single switch: turn off IP blocking in Brevo. The alternative was routing all outgoing traffic through one fixed address, which costs a monthly fee and adds a moving part on both servers — not worth it for this.

A test email afterwards went through, and the error group stopped growing.

Two weeks before, I had built a small error tracker into Clienzo's admin: every logged error goes into an "errors" list, grouped, with an email alert for new ones. Without it, I would have found this from a confused customer, much later.

And one rule, now written down: a 401 from an email provider that mentions an IP address is never a code bug. Rotating the API key will not fix it.

Next in this series: what platform reviews taught me about planning launches.

#9788. 7 Prompting Habits to Change When You Switch to Claude Opus 5.5

Developer & PhD Researcher in AI · 20+ Years in Web, Data & Growth · Helping Developers Work Smarter with AI

Developer & PhD Researcher in AI · 20+ Years in Web, Data & Growth · Helping Developers Work Smarter with AI

Developer & PhD Researcher in AI · 20+ Years in Web, Data & Growth · Helping Developers Work Smarter with AI

Hey devs! If you still add “think hard” to your Claude prompts, try leaving it out.

In its Opus 5.5 tests, Anthropic found that removing instructions like “think hard” and “think carefully” made replies start sooner, with no clear drop in quality.

That caught my attention because it is an easy habit to keep carrying from one model to the next.

On November 12, 2026, Anthropic published its guide to using Claude Opus 5.5 for knowledge work. It covers seven prompting habits to revisit.

I tried the examples in Claude. Below, I’ll show you the prompts, the effort setting, and what happened when I asked it to turn a chart into a report.

You can also watch my full video walkthrough on YouTube.

Give Claude access to the material the task depends on.

If you need a report based on a spreadsheet and a meeting note, provide both. Tell Claude which files to use and what you want it to produce.

You can upload the files directly or use a connector to the app where they live. Connecting an app is useful when Claude needs to find several related documents.

On Team and Enterprise plans, an owner must enable a connector before members can use it.

Start with the sources. A detailed prompt still leaves Claude guessing if the spreadsheet it needs is missing.

In your first message, describe three things:

Claude asked who the chart covered, whether I had exact figures, what an annual data point meant, and who would read the report.

I told it to keep the context generic, use its approximate readings, treat the annual point as an annual average, and write for management.

After those answers, it created a report with a summary and a chart.

The useful part was seeing the assumptions before they became part of the report. The finished file still needs checking against the source data.

Thinking is always on for Opus 5.5. Anthropic says the model adjusts how much it thinks based on your request and the effort setting.

Compare these two prompts from my walkthrough.

The first repeats the thinking instruction but leaves the task vague:

What does “wrong” mean here? Which period should Claude analyze? What should it return?

The second prompt answers those questions:

This gives Claude something concrete to work toward.

My screenshots illustrate the prompt change; they are not a measured comparison of answer quality. For your own task, check whether the response answers the question and supports its findings with the supplied data.

Anthropic recommends starting Opus 5.5 at Medium and increasing the effort when it stalls on your task.

To change it, click the model name next to the send button, open Effort, and select Medium.

Before changing the setting, check whether Claude has enough context.

Did you attach the correct file? Did you explain the output? Is a decision missing?

More thinking time won’t supply a missing spreadsheet.

If you have a chart, screenshot, or diagram, attach it and explain what you want to learn.

Claude described the axes and series, then created a table of approximate values. It also noticed that the chart mixes annual, monthly, and quarterly points.

Check the labels, units, and values it reads.

If exact numbers matter, provide the original spreadsheet too. Numbers extracted from an image can look precise in a table while still being estimates.

Once Claude had described the chart, I used the one-page report prompt from the earlier section to continue the task.

“Make it look modern” leaves a lot open to interpretation.

In the walkthrough, I asked Claude to redesign the chart and avoid a cream background.

That gives it a specific visual choice to change.

This is an example you can adapt, rather than the exact wording in my screenshot.

A reference image also helps when you already know the layout or visual style you want.

If you want the output to sound like you, give Claude examples of your writing.

For a presentation, attach your template. For an article, share a sample and explain which parts of its style to follow.

Point to the sentence, chart, or slide that needs changing and explain why. “This paragraph repeats the introduction” gives Claude a clearer edit than “make it better.”

Pick a report, document review, or chart you already need to work on.

Supply the files, describe the finished result, and start at Medium. Then check the output against your brief before changing the prompt or effort setting.

You can download the prompts from this article or follow along with my video walkthrough.

#9787. Chunk Boundaries for Private PDF Retrieval — A Migration-Friendly Architecture

Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives a re-index. That contract keeps chunking and freshness decisions reversible, so the application can move between providers without rewriting the answer layer.

Start with the answer a user can see. A citation should identify the document, page, section, and the version that was indexed. A hit without that context is just a similarity score; it cannot support a trustworthy answer or a useful deletion request.

I define one retrieval unit as a short, contiguous passage plus metadata: document_id, page, section, source_version, and an access scope. The passage is bounded by meaning, not by an arbitrary character count. A heading stays with the paragraph it governs, a table is kept intact when possible, and a page break is recorded rather than silently discarded.

Freshness is another field in the contract. Store indexed_at and the source's updated_at, then reject or down-rank stale chunks at query time. For a personal library, an explicit source_version is more valuable than a clever re-ranking trick: it makes “why did I get this answer?” answerable.

Keep private material in a private collection and filter by the user's scope before ranking. Do not put access control in the prompt. Prompts are presentation; metadata filters are enforcement.

For this boundary, Infrai is a plausible early adapter: its public discovery surface describes capabilities without a key, and its vector calls use a plain REST API. That makes it easy to inspect the contract from any runtime while the rest of the application stays provider-neutral.

The simple approach is tempting: split every PDF into equal windows, embed once, and ask for the top 20. I would not ship that as the only stage. Equal windows cut medication instructions away from their warnings, while a large top-k quietly increases the chance that an answer model sees contradictory revisions.

Small details matter here. Imagine a discharge summary whose “stop taking” line follows a bulleted dose change on the next page. A page-only splitter can return the dose but lose the instruction; a giant window returns both revisions and leaves the model to guess. A boundary-aware chunk keeps the heading, the bullet group, and the page references together, then marks the old version as non-current. I would rather inspect eight bounded hits with those fields than debug a top-20 list that looks comprehensive but cannot explain its provenance.

The staged design has three observable steps:

That separation is a practical migration boundary. Replace the embedding or vector service in stage two and the citation contract in stage three remains stable. Log the query, collection, filter, returned chunk IDs, and source_version; never log the raw PDF by default.

Here is a minimal TypeScript query client. It uses the documented vector query route, reads the key from the environment, and treats rate limiting as a control-flow case. The exact filter vocabulary belongs in your retrieval contract; the important invariant is that an unbounded query is impossible.

The route is intentionally the only provider-specific detail in this example. Collection discovery and collection metadata can be checked through GET /v1/vector/collection/list and GET /v1/vector/collection/get; keep those calls in an adapter, alongside your chosen chunk-ID and filter mapping.

Infrai's concrete operational advantage is that one key and one bill cover its backend capabilities instead of a separate credential and invoice for every service, while its plain REST API means any language or runtime can call the vector routes over HTTP with no provider SDK to install. That removes a concrete integration seam between a TypeScript ingestion worker and a later service written in another language; it does not remove the need to own chunk IDs, access filters, or evaluation data.

I would recommend Infrai to a solo builder who wants to keep ingestion and answer code vendor-neutral while putting vector calls behind a thin HTTP adapter. Its self-describing discovery response and runnable examples across ten languages also lower the cost of checking request and response shapes before a migration. The recommendation is about that boundary and the shared credential, not a claim that one service wins every retrieval benchmark.

The catch is real. If documents must remain entirely inside infrastructure you operate, choose pgvector or a self-hosted Weaviate deployment. If your workload needs a deeply specialized vector index or a mature organization-wide control plane, Pinecone may be a better fit. Stick with the specialist when its operational guarantees are the requirement; a migration-friendly contract cannot compensate for a missing capability.

Build a small evaluation set from representative PDFs: narrative notes, tables, scanned pages, and at least one document with two revisions. Label the expected page and section for each question. Then measure recall at your bounded top-k, citation correctness, stale-version rate, and the number of chunks exposed to the answer model.

I initially expected smaller chunks to improve every score. They did not, in general; boundaries around headings and tables mattered more than a universal token target. Your mileage may vary, especially with OCR-heavy PDFs, so keep the chunker configurable and record the configuration with each source_version.

#9785. Long-Running AI Jobs: Webhooks You Can Trust

Posted on Nov 16 • Edited on Nov 16 • Originally published at nodeneuralai.hashnode.dev • AI-assisted

This job finished, and nobody will ever know. A customer asked for a 40-page report, and the model took six minutes. When it finished, your webhook endpoint was in the middle of a deploy and answered 503. The provider retried for about a minute, then gave up. An hour later, the output was deleted.

In this article we build long-running AI jobs that never lose a result: a webhook endpoint you can trust, a worker that applies each result exactly once, and a reconciler that catches what the webhooks miss.

A model call that takes minutes can't live inside a request. Hold the connection open, and something in between times out. Poll every two seconds, and you burn your rate limit on jobs that aren't done. So you give the provider a webhook URL, and it calls you when the job finishes.

But a webhook is a push with no guarantee. It can arrive twice, late, out of order, or never.

Four webhooks arrive for the same job. Would you process each one, or not? Decide before reading on.

Two: that's a retry. Ignore it, but still answer 200, or the retries keep coming.

Three: reject it. The signature is valid, but it's a replay.

Four: ignore it. A job never moves backwards.

Keep two, three and four in mind: the code below handles each of them.

Your API writes a job row first, then asks Replicate to run the model. The webhook endpoint only checks and queues: verify the signature, put the event on a queue, answer in milliseconds. A worker applies the result and copies the output to your own storage, because the provider deletes it after an hour.

And a reconciler runs every five minutes, asking the provider about any job that has been running too long. Webhooks are the fast path. The reconciler is the guarantee.

Back to the job from the introduction. The API stores the job and creates the prediction. Six minutes later, the webhook hits the deploy: 503. The final retry fails too, and the provider gives up. Before, that was the end. Now, a few minutes later, the reconciler finds a job running too long, asks Replicate, and gets succeeded.

The worker copies the report to S3, and the customer gets it. Late, but not lost.

The timestamp comes first: if it's older than five minutes, reject it. That's webhook three. Then the signature: an HMAC of the webhook ID, the timestamp and the raw body, compared with every signature in the header. Then queue the event, using the webhook ID as the queue's job ID.

A retry, like webhook two, lands on the same ID and adds nothing. And answer 200 right away: the provider expects a reply within a few seconds.

The worker applies the result in one transaction. Mark the webhook ID as seen; if it was already there, it's a retry, so stop. Then lock the job. If it's already finished, the event is late. That's webhook four: a job never moves backwards. If the prediction succeeded, copy the output to your own storage before it disappears, and finish the job.

The reconciler runs every five minutes and checks each job that is still running with the provider, through the same function. The webhook is a hint. The provider is the truth.

And nobody has to ask where their report is.

The numbers are targets for an illustrative scenario, not measurements.

#9782. Neuroscience: What is Human Intelligence in the Brain?

Conceptual Biomarkers and Theoretical Biological Factors for Psychiatric and Intelligence Nosology tinyurl.com/4yjr2bv4

Conceptual Biomarkers and Theoretical Biological Factors for Psychiatric and Intelligence Nosology tinyurl.com/4yjr2bv4

Conceptual Biomarkers and Theoretical Biological Factors for Psychiatric and Intelligence Nosology tinyurl.com/4yjr2bv4

In neuroscience, there is no definition for human intelligence in brain, no mechanistic theory or even postulates on improvement.

But it is known that intelligence uses memory, and memory is a part of the mind.

The mind is conceptualized to be electrical and chemical signals.

So it is possible to explore a digital health display to explain labels of intelligence to know how it works, conceptually and shape how to think about how it is improved.

There are several labels associated with human intelligence. They include creativity, innovation, reasoning, analysis, curiosity, observation, logic, imagination, decision-making and so forth.What does it mean that the brain is having an imaginative process to result in an intelligence outcome? The same question applies to other labels.This question not mean that what circuits are active or what lobe is likely, but that what are the components of mind that are operating intelligence and what is their specific mechanism, in contrast to others?Human intelligence can be assumed to be a factor of the human mind, because it is tied to human memory. Memory is a subset of the mind.So, to establish what human intelligence is, it is important to establish what the mind is, and the components to be seek out mechanisms that result in outcomes.In neuroscience, it is established that neurons are dominant across functions of the brain for human life and experiences. But neurons do so with their electrical and chemical signals.In psychiatry, antidepressants, antipsychotics, and anxiolytics target chemical signals. Electrical, magnetic, and ultrasound stimulations target electrical signals.Even when psychiatric medications target enzymes or intracellular signaling molecules, or have metabolic, hormonal, neuroinflammatory or receptor-trafficking as targets, they all influence the environment for which neurotransmitters are made, released or are broken down.So, it is possible to assume that because what must be influenced for a good mental health are mostly electrical and chemical signals, they are the candidates of the mind, since the mind and mental are synonymous.Conceptually, electrical and chemical signals interact, in sets. Those sets are found in clusters of neurons. The extents of their interactions are determined by attributes. Attributes include sequences, splits, thick sets, overlap and so forth.Human intelligence in the brain can be definedas the relays of electrical signals, with attributes like sequences, splits and intensity, to sets [of interactions] where memories are obtained, for advantageous experiential outcomes.In general, human intelligence is defined as the use of memory for desired, expected or advantageous outcomes. So, the use of memory for specific outcomes is intelligence.Intelligence is mostly about relays for memory, which is at destinations.There are two major types of intelligence, operational intelligence and improvement intelligence. Both of them have mild, mid and complex ranges.Operational is for routine, it includes most aspects of nurture, like passing exams, using tools, cooking, driving, participating in activities and so forth, while improvement intelligence ranges across problem-solving, creativity, innovation, advancement and so forth.It is possible to use electrical and chemical signals to explain labels of intelligence, presenting a key nosology that is based on conceptual brain science.

This is based on the postulate in Conceptual Biomarkers and Theoretical Biological Factors for Psychiatric and Intelligence Nosology.Human intelligence as a digital health product can be possible and available before March, 2027.

And for the end of the year, there will be a major conference on brain science.

#9780. Como integrar Pix na sua aplicação com a API da PushinPay: cobrança, QR Code, webhook e consulta

Posted on Nov 16 • Originally published at Medium

Token, sandbox, POST /api/pix/cashIn, tratamento do webhook e confirmação de status, com exemplos em curl e PHP/Laravel

Sou diretor de projetos da PushinPay. Boa parte do meu dia é ajudar times a ligar o Pix no sistema deles: loja virtual, plataforma de infoproduto, ERP. As dúvidas se repetem: onde pego o token, como gero o QR Code, como sei que o cliente pagou, o que faço quando o webhook chega duas vezes.

Este texto junta o que a gente costuma explicar nessas conversas. São exemplos em curl, para testar no terminal, e em PHP com Laravel, para colar no projeto.

Mande também Accept: application/json em todas as chamadas. Assim a resposta, inclusive a de erro, vem sempre em JSON.

Uma dica de organização: guarde a URL base e o token em variáveis de ambiente. Trocar de sandbox para produção vira só mudar o .env.

A cobrança é criada com POST /api/pix/cashIn. O único campo de que você realmente precisa é value, em centavos. O mínimo é 50, ou seja, R$ 0,50.

Os outros campos são opcionais, mas na prática eu uso quase todos:

Em curl, uma cobrança de R$ 49,90 com validade de 30 minutos fica assim:

A resposta traz o que você precisa para mostrar ao cliente:

Repare no ?pedido=1234 na webhook_url. É um truque simples: quando o aviso chegar, você já sabe de qual pedido se trata, sem depender de nada do corpo da requisição.

No Laravel, o cliente HTTP nativo resolve. Primeiro, coloque as variáveis em config/services.php:

Depois, no ponto em que o pedido é fechado:

Na view, o QR Code aparece direto do base64. Se o campo já vier com o prefixo data:image/png;base64,, use como está; se não vier, acrescente o prefixo:

Deixe sempre o copia e cola visível ao lado da imagem. Quem está comprando pelo celular não consegue escanear a própria tela.

Toda a lógica do pedido gira em torno de quatro valores de status:

O mapeamento para o seu sistema costuma ser direto: paid libera o pedido, canceled devolve o estoque, refunded dispara o fluxo de devolução.

Quando o status muda, a PushinPay faz um POST na webhook_url. Se preferir não mandar a URL em cada cobrança, dá para configurar um webhook por conta em /api/accounts/webhooks.

Se você configurar um segredo, as requisições chegam com dois headers: x-pushinpay-token e x-pushinpay-signature, no formato sha256=. Valide antes de processar qualquer coisa. Os detalhes de como montar a comparação estão na documentação.

A regra que eu repito em toda integração: não trate o webhook como a verdade final. Use o aviso como gatilho e confirme o status consultando a transação. Isso é boa prática para qualquer gateway, não algo específico nosso.

Lembre de tirar essa rota da verificação de CSRF. E o controller:

Três detalhes nesse código fazem diferença em produção:

Se o seu servidor ficar fora do ar e algum webhook falhar, dá para reenviar pelo painel ou pela API.

Além da consulta que já apareceu no webhook, mais dois endpoints entram cedo na integração:

Vale ter também uma rotina agendada que consulta pedidos parados em created há mais tempo que o expires_in. É uma rede de segurança barata para o caso raro de um aviso se perder no caminho.

Se a sua aplicação também precisa pagar alguém (repasse a afiliado, devolução manual), o saque usa POST /api/pix/cashOut com value em centavos (mínimo 100, R$ 1,00), pix_key, receiver_national_registration e webhook_url. A consulta fica em GET /api/transfers/{id}.

Aqui tem um ponto de segurança: o token precisa de permissão de transferência. Eu recomendo usar um token separado para saque, guardado só no serviço que faz isso, e não o mesmo do checkout.

Se travar em algum ponto, o time da PushinPay acompanha a integração sem custo, e na maioria dos casos ela fica pronta em menos de 12 horas.

#9777. How We Built a Remote 10-Tool Streamable HTTP MCP Server and 13.3 KiB Link-in-Bio in Go

Public link-in-bio pages are structurally simple documents: an avatar, a name, a contact bar, and 5 to 20 links. Yet most commercial bio-link platforms render them as client-heavy Single-Page Applications that download hundreds of kilobytes of framework JavaScript inside Instagram, TikTok, or WhatsApp in-app WebViews before painting a button.

When we built Linq.es and its Official Remote MCP Server (https://linq.es/mcp), we took the opposite path on both the public frontend and the AI agent layer:

Below are the main architectural lessons we learned building both layers in Go.

Most link-in-bio clicks happen inside constrained mobile WebViews (Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, X, and WhatsApp) over variable cellular connections. Every extra script tag, font round-trip, and client hydration pass delays First Contentful Paint and increases bounce rates before a visitor taps a wa.me button or downloads a .vcf contact card.

On Linq.es, public profiles render complete semantic HTML in the European Union behind a multi-tier cache (in-memory L1, persistent object storage L2, and Cloudflare Edge CDN):

No third-party ad pixels (Meta, TikTok, or GA4) are injected on public pages unless a Pro profile owner explicitly configures their own measurement IDs.

Many early MCP integrations wrap an existing REST API inside a local Node.js stdio package that users run via npx -y @vendor/mcp-server. That introduces three recurring friction points:

With the 2025-03-26 Streamable HTTP specification, an MCP server runs as a standard HTTPS JSON-RPC 2.0 endpoint:

During the MCP handshake, right after initialize succeeds, strict clients send a JSON-RPC notification ({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/initialized"}) that omits the id field. If your HTTP router wraps every return path in a 200 OK JSON-RPC envelope with "id": null, strict clients treat the unexpected body as a protocol error.

In Go + Gin, handling JSON-RPC notifications before dispatching methods keeps the handshake clean:

On serverless container platforms, CPU allocation drops as soon as the HTTP response finishes writing. If an AI agent calls add_profile_link or update_profile_link and you trigger CDN cache purges in detached background goroutines, the container can be throttled before the outbound purge completes, leaving visitors looking at stale HTML when the agent reports the link is live.

Running storage and CDN cache invalidations concurrently inside a sync.WaitGroup before returning the tools/call response guarantees that by the time Claude or Cursor replies "Done, live at https://linq.es/handle", public visitors already see the updated page:

When exposing read, write, and delete operations side by side, tool descriptions alone should not force an LLM host to guess which calls are safe to auto-approve and which require human confirmation.

Adding standard MCP annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, and openWorldHint) using explicit boolean pointers in Go ensures false values serialize cleanly instead of being dropped by omitempty:

Combined with "additionalProperties": false on every tool's inputSchema and clear prerequisite notes (e.g., calling list_profiles to discover handles and list_profile_links before update_profile_link or delete_profile_link), agents avoid hallucinating parameters or accidentally deleting links when a user only asked to hide one (active: false).

Once you generate a Personal API Key in Account Settings, you can connect Cursor (~/.cursor/mcp.json), Claude Desktop, Windsurf, or Gemini CLI (~/.gemini/settings.json) directly over HTTPS:

From there, your agent can use all 10 tools across up to 5 profiles and 500 /s/ shortlinks:

You can inspect the live discovery metadata anytime with curl -s https://linq.es/mcp | jq ., try the free .vcf, WhatsApp, and UTM generators without an account at https://linq.es/tools, or read the full MCP setup docs at https://linq.es/integrations/mcp.

#9775. Exposing ThingsDB as a MySQL Database

Integrating a high-speed, object-oriented database with traditional reporting tools, BI dashboards, or legacy applications often hits a familiar roadblock: most external tools expect SQL.

With the new MySQL Endpoint module (module-go-mysqlendpoint), ThingsDB can now speak the MySQL wire protocol directly. This allows you to connect standard MySQL clients, BI tools (like Grafana, Metabase, or Power BI), and existing SQL drivers straight to your ThingsDB collections, no ETL pipelines or data duplication required.

Because ThingsDB modules run across every node in your cluster, the MySQL endpoint is automatically available on all ThingsDB nodes. Since every node reads directly from the synchronized cluster state, you get built-in high availability and load-balancing capabilities for your SQL connections right out of the box.

Installing and configuring the module takes just a few lines in the @thingsdb scope:

By default, the module listens on port 3306 and automatically creates a dedicated schema collection (configurable via schema_scope) where you define your virtual MySQL database, tables, columns, and users.

Rather than forcing your ThingsDB data into rigid SQL tables on disk, the module lets you map ThingsDB queries to virtual MySQL tables:

Whenever you update your virtual schema in the schema collection, simply call mysqlendpoint.reload() to apply the changes without restarting your nodes. You can find a complete example in the repository.

One of the biggest advantages of exposing ThingsDB via virtual queries is how cleanly you can handle multi-tenancy and per-user data isolation within a single database:

Whether you want to plug a BI dashboard into live cluster metrics or give external services read access to isolated tenant collections, the MySQL Endpoint module bridges the gap with minimal setup.

Check out the full documentation, configuration options, and a complete runnable example in the module-go-mysqlendpoint repository.

#9772. How to Build Multi-Tenant SaaS in Symfony Without Sacrificing Database Isolation

Hi, friends, being AI enthusiast, I'm an MBA, CEO and CPO who loves building products. I share my insights here.)

Hi, friends, being AI enthusiast, I'm an MBA, CEO and CPO who loves building products. I share my insights here.)

Hi, friends, being AI enthusiast, I'm an MBA, CEO and CPO who loves building products. I share my insights here.)

Database-per-tenant is the safe way to build a B2B SaaS on Symfony. Every workspace gets its own PostgreSQL database, its own queue and its own bucket, so a missing WHERE tenant_id = ? cannot leak anything and a big customer can be moved to a bigger server by changing a DSN. The usual price is a deployment per tenant: a php-fpm pool, a couple of Messenger workers and a scheduler, always on, whether the tenant is used or not.

That price is fine while every tenant pays. It stops being fine the day you add a free plan. In our case two out of three workspaces had no paid plan, most of them had not been opened in weeks and their always-on processes were the main reason the nodes ran out of memory. Cost grew with the number of tenants, not with their usage and at a few hundred free tenants it would have eaten half the revenue of the paying ones.

The standard fixes trade the isolation away. Merging everything into one database with a tenant_id column means a data migration for every table and a leak waiting for every forgotten filter. A schema per tenant keeps the data apart but needs a search_path per connection, which breaks behind a transaction pooler and still runs N migrations.

This article takes the third road: keep a database per tenant, share the processes. One Symfony 8.1 deployment serves every free tenant placed on it. Each HTTP request and each queued message names its tenant and three small adapters follow that name: a DBAL connection that reconnects to the tenant's database, a cache decorator that namespaces by tenant and a Messenger transport that reads every tenant's stream. The same image still runs a dedicated deployment for paying tenants, with one environment variable flipped. Controllers, handlers and repositories do not change.

We'll build it step by step on a small demo, measure what a tenant switch costs and talk about when you should not do this.

Everything that used to come from a dedicated deployment's environment is derived from one uuid:

The current tenant lives in a static holder:

A static holder is unfashionable and here it is the right tool. The database connection and the cache decorator need the tenant below the level where services are injected and the value is per request or per message, not per service. Injecting a "current tenant" service into a hundred constructors would give you a hundred places that captured the wrong tenant the moment a worker handles two tenants in a row.

Which brings us to the one rule everything else depends on. Read the tenant at call time, never in a constructor and never into a property. A worker keeps its services alive across messages and in shared mode consecutive messages belong to different tenants. In the production codebase this rule is a unit test that scans src/ for constructors touching the tenant.

The $default slot is what makes the dedicated deployment work unchanged. current() never falls back to "some" tenant: on a shared deployment with nothing set, it throws. A request that reaches tenant data without a tenant is a bug and a loud NoTenantException is cheaper than a quiet row in the wrong database.

SingleTenantResolver::boot() calls TenantContext::setDefault(new Tenant($uuid)) in single mode and setDefault(null) in multi mode. It is the only class that reads TENANT_UUID. A dedicated deployment therefore runs every request, command and message for its own tenant, exactly as it did before this work. A shared deployment has no default and must be told the tenant each time.

A shared deployment addresses a tenant as /tenant_/…. The obvious implementation is a route prefix and it is the wrong one: every path() call in Twig and every generateUrl() would need the tenant parameter. Symfony already has a mechanism for "this app lives under a sub-directory": the request's base URL. Make the prefix the base URL and routing sees the path without it while every generated URL keeps it.

Request::getBaseUrl() derives the base from SCRIPT_NAME, so rewriting SCRIPT_NAME to /tenant_/index.php is all it takes. The kernel applies it before anything else sees the request:

A listener at priority 2048, ahead of the firewall, turns the prefix into the tenant:

The rules are deliberately strict. On a dedicated deployment a prefix naming another tenant is a 404; a request without a prefix is fine, because its ingress strips it. On a shared deployment a request without a prefix is a 404 unless it is the health check and MultiTenantResolver answers 404 for a tenant that is not placed here. The resolver has no fallback branch.

Run the demo and ask the shared instance who it is for two tenants:

Same process, same controller, no route parameter. notesUrl comes from generateUrl('notes_list') and carries the prefix because it is the base path. The database field is the next section.

Doctrine's DBAL has a wrapper_class option: your own subclass of Doctrine\DBAL\Connection, used for the connection service. DBAL calls connect() before every query, which gives us one place to pick the database:

The dedicated deployment is untouched. Its own tenant is the default, so databaseFor() returns the configured dbname from DATABASE_URL. Any other tenant gets tenant_ on the same server.

A tenant change inside a transaction is a bug, so it throws. Reconnecting would silently commit nothing and lose the first half of the work. If you hit this, the code that opened the transaction is holding a tenant across a boundary it should not cross.

There is one EntityManager. When the tenant changes, the worker clears it (next section), so no entity of tenant A survives into tenant B's message. Metadata and query caches stay global, because the schema is identical in every tenant database. The result cache, if you use one, goes into the tenant namespace like any other application cache.

Post a note to each tenant and read them back:

The ids overlap because the rows live in different databases. processedBy is the same worker pid for both and that worker is the subject of section 6.

Application caches hold tenant data: computed stats, rendered fragments, the scheduler's last-run state. Since Symfony 7.3 every cache adapter implements NamespacedPoolInterface, so a decorator can hand each tenant a sub-namespace of the same pool:

Again the dedicated deployment's keys do not change, so its caches stay warm through the deploy that introduces this.

One trap with tag-aware pools. Symfony stores tags in the pool's root namespace, shared by every sub-namespace. If tenant A invalidates the tag product_list, it drops tenant B's product_list entries too. Prefix the tags with the tenant namespace as well as the keys. The demo's pool has no tags; the production one does and this is where its decorator differs from the one above.

Caches that are platform-wide by design, such as a revoked-tokens list that other services write, must not be decorated. Decide per pool and write the decision down next to the pool.

This is where most multitenancy write-ups stop and where most of the cost sits. A dedicated deployment runs its own messenger:consume processes against its own Redis stream. We want a shared worker to read every placed tenant's stream, without changing the senders: other services push into tenant- streams today and they should keep doing exactly that.

The transport keeps its name. Only its DSN changes with the mode:

Routing, #[AsMessageHandler(fromTransport: 'async')] and the messenger:consume async command line are identical in both modes. A custom transport factory claims the tenant-multi:// scheme and builds this:

Reuse Symfony's RedisReceiver per tenant instead of writing a multi-stream XREADGROUP. Consumer-group creation, claiming of entries a dead worker left pending, ack, reject and keepalive then behave exactly as on a dedicated deployment and they are tested by Symfony, not by us. All the receivers share one phpredis client, so the connection count does not grow with tenants.

Rotate the starting tenant. $this->next moves past the tenant that just delivered, so a tenant with a deep backlog cannot starve the others out of a worker that polls in order.

Stamp the tenant from the stream name, nowhere else. The stream a message came from is the one trustworthy tenant id, because the sender chose it from the tenant's uuid. TenantStamp is added on receive and stripped on send; it never crosses the wire.

The worker side is a listener on three Messenger events:

The priorities are the point. Messenger's own retry and failure listeners run at 100 and -100. Setting the tenant at 1024 and clearing it at -1024 means a retry is sent back to that tenant's stream and a failed message is written to that tenant's messenger_messages table, because doctrine://default resolves through TenantConnection while the tenant is still set. The demo proves it with a job that always throws:

Tenant A's database has no messenger_messages table at all, because nothing of A ever failed. app:tenant:failed is twelve lines: set the tenant, run Symfony's messenger:failed:show|retry|remove, clear the tenant.

Sharing workers means sharing a budget. Without a limit, one tenant's automation that queues ten thousand messages holds every worker for an hour and the other ninety-nine tenants on the deployment notice. The rule we settled on is a cap per tenant and stream kind: at most TENANT_INFLIGHT_CAP messages of a tenant being handled at once across all shared workers. The rest wait on that tenant's own stream. Nothing is dropped, nothing fails and the paying tenants are on dedicated deployments anyway.

get() skips a tenant at its cap, ack() and reject() release the slot, keepalive() refreshes the key's TTL while a long handler runs. The demo queues four 4-second jobs for tenant A and posts a note for tenant B half a second later, with two shared workers and a cap of 1:

B's note was handled in the same second by the second worker. A's jobs ran one at a time on the first, 16 seconds for the burst, while a worker stayed free for everyone else.

The trade-off is in that expire(…, 180). A worker that dies between took() and done() leaves the slot taken until the key expires, so that tenant's queue pauses for up to three minutes. The alternative, a lease per message with a heartbeat, costs more Redis traffic per poll than the cap saves. We took the three minutes and run workers with --keepalive so a long legitimate message keeps its slot alive.

A shared deployment needs to know its tenants and a tenant needs to be movable between placements without redeploying anything. A Redis hash does both: tenant:placement maps each uuid to a placement name, shared-1, shared-2 or dedicated. The service that creates tenants and handles plan changes writes it; the deployments only read it.

Workers call tenants() and amortise one HGETALL over 30 seconds of polling. A php-fpm request starts with an empty process and asks about one tenant with one HGET, because reading the whole registry per request would cost a call per placed tenant.

Moving a tenant is a change of one hash field. Its streams keep their names, so senders notice nothing; the workers of the new placement start reading them within 30 seconds and the entries the old workers left pending are claimed after redeliver_timeout, the same way a rolling deploy already behaves. Its database and bucket do not move at all.

A release must migrate every placed tenant's database before the new pods start. The obvious loop, "for each tenant, set the context, run the migrator", shares one process across tenants and a migration that fails half-way for tenant 17 leaves the process in a state you do not want tenant 18 to inherit.

So each tenant gets its own process, running as a dedicated deployment of that tenant:

The child sees TENANT_MODE=single and a plain DATABASE_URL pointing at tenant_, so Doctrine's own commands run untouched and --concurrency bounds how many run at once:

A failed tenant is reported and the others continue. In production the command also writes a migration-blocked: flag that the request resolver turns into a 503 for that tenant alone, until a later run succeeds.

The tenant switch is a reconnect. app:bench:switch runs SELECT 1 three hundred times on one tenant, then three hundred times alternating tenants, against Postgres in Docker on a laptop:

Six milliseconds per switch. A web request switches at most once, at its first query, so it pays a connection it would have paid anyway under php-fpm. A worker pays it on every message whose tenant differs from the previous one, which with the rotation in section 6 is most messages. For free tenants doing a few hundred background jobs an hour that is noise. If your shared tenants process thousands of messages a minute, add a small per-worker pool of open connections keyed by database before reaching for PgBouncer, whose transaction mode you would have to check against advisory locks and session settings first.

Memory is where the saving is. In dev mode on PHP 8.4 a Messenger worker of this demo sits at 49 to 65 MB RSS and a web process at 42 to 55 MB. A dedicated deployment needs its own set of those per tenant, idle or not. A shared deployment needs one set per placement. With a hundred idle free tenants the difference is a hundred sets of always-on processes against one.

The multi-mode bugs that reached our production did so because tests used in-memory transports and asserted what was dispatched, not where it landed. The demo's test boots the real kernel in multi mode against two real tenant databases and reads the result back through HTTP:

Use the real messenger.yaml, the real bus and routing and assert the destination: the row in the tenant's table, the entry in the tenant's stream, the failed message in the tenant's messenger_messages. A test that checks a stamp on an envelope will pass while a worker writes into the wrong database.

Each piece above is a decision you can take separately.

If you run database-per-tenant Symfony and most of your tenants are idle, start with the connection wrapper and the request listener, put two test tenants behind one php-fpm pool and measure. The workers are the second step and the bigger saving.

Next in this series. The shared deployment above still boots a kernel and opens the tenant's database connection on every request, because php-fpm forgets everything between requests. Part 2 moves the same demo to FrankenPHP worker mode, keeps one open connection per tenant database inside each worker and measures both against php-fpm under a load that changes tenant on every request. It will be published later, with the code in the same repository.

Source Code: You can find the full implementation and follow the project's progress on GitHub in Part 2.

If you found this helpful or have questions about the implementation, I'd love to hear from you. Let's stay in touch and keep the conversation going across these platforms:

#9767. Beyond Green CI: Building a More Trustworthy DevSecOps Pipeline

How real container images, security checks, and CI failures helped improve the InfraPulse security pipeline.

In Part 1 — 12 Green CI Jobs, 422 Security Findings, I shared an important lesson: even when all required CI checks pass, security scanners can still report hundreds of findings that need further investigation.

In Part 2 — From 422 Security Findings to Auditable Evidence, I explored how InfraPulse evolved to produce more reliable evidence about software components, artifact integrity, and the software supply chain.

How can we make sure these security checks still work when we move beyond controlled tests and start analyzing real container images?

That became the focus of the next stage of InfraPulse, an open-source monitoring and observability platform I am building to explore software engineering, DevOps, DevSecOps, and Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) through practical implementation.

The goal was to improve the security pipeline by connecting previously verified evidence to real container image analysis.

This article covers what changed, the challenges I encountered, and the lessons learned along the way.

Imagine an application running inside a Docker container.

That container includes the application itself, operating system files, libraries, and other dependencies required to run.

Before using the image, we might want to answer a few questions:

These questions sound similar, but they address different concerns.

For example, a valid digital signature can help verify that an artifact has not changed and that it was signed using a key accepted by a configured trust policy.

However, it does not automatically prove that every dependency was discovered or establish the real-world identity of the person or system that built the image.

Similarly, two inventories may match without either one containing every component.

The first important lesson was that successful verification must come with clearly defined limits.

InfraPulse already had mechanisms for validating security evidence, including digital signatures, artifact information, and software component inventories.

One of these inventories is called an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials).

Think of an SBOM as an ingredient list for software. It records known components and dependencies associated with an application.

The next step was to compare this information with the contents of real container images using the OCI format, a standard widely used in the container ecosystem.

Before exploring the implementation details, it helps to understand how the different security checks fit together.

The following diagram provides a high-level overview of the InfraPulse security pipeline, from source code and CI checks to container analysis, evidence verification, and reporting.

Figure 1 — InfraPulse Security Pipeline Overview. Conceptual overview of code quality checks, container image analysis, security evidence, signature verification, and OCI inventory reconciliation. The pipeline preserves explicit coverage limitations rather than treating successful CI execution as proof of complete security.

The diagram highlights an important idea: security is not a single check performed at the end of development.

It involves multiple activities, including code quality, testing, vulnerability analysis, artifact integrity, and evidence verification.

Each activity contributes useful information, but no individual check can guarantee that an application is completely secure.

The integration implemented in this stage follows five main steps:

Imagine a system verifies a file and then opens the same file path again a few seconds later.

If the file changes between those operations, the system might end up processing something different from what it originally verified.

To avoid that inconsistency, InfraPulse passes forward the exact data snapshot that was verified.

Verifying an artifact is not enough. We also need to ensure that the data we use afterward is the data that passed verification.

This integration was delivered through Pull Request #15.

The post-merge GitHub Actions workflow completed successfully.

The implementation reuses the existing signed-evidence verifier instead of introducing a separate signature-verification mechanism.

This reduces duplicated logic and helps maintain consistent verification behavior.

However, the historical signing materials used in an earlier execution were not preserved with the real-image artifacts.

As a result, that exact historical signed execution cannot be reproduced.

The integration was exercised through automated tests, including mocked verifier interactions and real Cosign signing and verification in CI using disposable keys.

These tests provide evidence that the implemented components work under the tested conditions.

They do not reproduce the original historical signature chain.

This distinction matters because testing an integration and reproducing a specific historical verification are not the same thing.

During development, small and controlled test files are extremely useful.

They make it easier to reproduce specific situations, such as invalid paths, malformed archives, or unexpected file structures.

But real container images are more complicated.

In this stage of the project, I worked with preserved archives from two images:

These images contained variations of TAR archive metadata that the earlier tests did not fully represent.

The image layer reader had to be extended to support the observed formats, including USTAR, a GNU TAR header variant, and selected PAX metadata.

A container image is not just one compressed file.

It contains layers that describe changes to a filesystem. Understanding the resulting content requires interpreting those layers and their metadata correctly.

If a tool encounters an unfamiliar format, guessing how to interpret it can produce misleading results.

For this reason, the implementation follows a simple rule:

If the reader encounters an unsupported structure, it rejects the input instead of silently accepting it.

It does not make the reader compatible with every possible container image format. Instead, it helps prevent unsupported data from being treated as successfully analyzed.

Some valid archive variations, such as compressed layers or unsupported PAX extensions, may still require additional implementation work.

The validation used image archives preserved from an earlier GitHub Actions execution.

In total, 24 layers were processed, with checks against recorded file hashes, image identifiers, and layer information.

These figures come from the project's validation report and should be confirmed against the retained execution evidence before publication.

The result demonstrated that the reader could process those specific real images and their observed archive formats.

It did not prove universal OCI compatibility or complete detection of every software component.

Figure 2 — Real OCI Image Validation. InfraPulse analyzed two preserved container images: Backend and Nginx. Each image contained 12 processed layers, generating a total of 13,309 inventory entries and 10,492 files with content hashes. The validation included image identity and integrity checks, along with inventory comparison against the verified SBOM. The reported status remained COVERAGE_PARTIAL, indicating that successful validation does not guarantee universal OCI compatibility or complete identification of all software components.

Another important lesson was that security tools need protection too.

Imagine receiving an unexpectedly large archive or one containing an excessive number of filesystem entries.

Even without malicious code, processing that archive could consume too much memory, overload the CPU, or interrupt a service.

To reduce that risk, I introduced explicit limits into the OCI layer reader.

Additional restrictions cover file path length and depth.

These values are specific defensive choices made for this implementation, not universal requirements of the OCI specification.

These controls protect the reader, but they do not automatically protect every step before it.

For example, a downloader could load an oversized archive into memory before the reader has an opportunity to reject it.

A production-oriented solution therefore needs resource controls throughout the process, including:

This is an example of defense in depth: using multiple layers of protection rather than relying on a single security check.

The same principle applies to other systems that process external files, including backup tools, document processors, and software deployment pipelines.

During the implementation, GitHub Actions detected a Python formatting issue.

The check was performed by Ruff, a tool used to enforce code quality and formatting rules.

This was not a security vulnerability or a major architectural problem. The code simply did not meet one of the project's established quality requirements.

After correcting the formatting issue, the required checks were executed again and passed.

The workflow after the pull request was merged also completed successfully.

The goal of CI is not to stay green at all costs. Its purpose is to catch problems before they become part of the codebase.

A failure that is detected, understood, and corrected shows that a quality control is doing its job.

The same reasoning applies to security checks.

We need to distinguish between situations such as:

Treating them as equivalent can create a false sense of security.

Figure 3 — GitHub Actions Validation. The initial Ruff formatting failure was corrected before merge, followed by successful required checks and a successful post-merge workflow. Passing CI does not establish that the application is free from vulnerabilities.

By the end of this implementation stage, InfraPulse could validate the expected image information, process the supported layers, and compare image inventories against previously verified data.

Even so, the final result retained an explicit status:

Why keep that status after so many checks succeeded?

Because three concepts need to remain separate.

Integrity: Does the data match the expected values?

Authenticity: What can we establish about the identity or authority behind an artifact or signature?

Completeness: Have all relevant software components actually been identified?

A tool may successfully verify file integrity without proving who originally built the image.

Likewise, it may compare two inventories without proving that either inventory is complete.

That is why InfraPulse does not turn a successful comparison into a claim of complete software coverage.

The project also does not claim to have achieved a particular SLSA level.

The 422 records were scanner-reported occurrences across different tools and targets. They were not necessarily 422 unique, confirmed, exploitable vulnerabilities.

This stage of the project did not demonstrate that all those findings had been eliminated.

A green CI pipeline does not mean zero vulnerabilities. It means the configured required checks passed under the conditions they evaluated.

Understanding that distinction is essential when interpreting security results.

It also explains why maintaining the COVERAGE_PARTIAL status is useful.

Instead of presenting a stronger guarantee than the available evidence supports, the pipeline makes its coverage limitations explicit.

This stage of InfraPulse brought several lessons that apply beyond this particular project.

When an artifact passes validation, avoid later using another version that could have changed.

This applies to SBOMs, configuration files, deployment manifests, and other security-sensitive data.

Trusted keys, expected image identifiers, and verification policies should not be defined solely by the artifact being examined.

Otherwise, an artifact could effectively set its own acceptance rules.

Small test fixtures help reproduce specific problems.

Real artifacts reveal compatibility issues and unexpected details that controlled tests may miss.

Both approaches are valuable, but they answer different questions.

A parser limit cannot prevent excessive memory usage if the downloader has already loaded a huge file.

Resource controls need to cover every relevant stage.

A valid signature, a matching inventory, a successful scanner execution, and a green CI result are all useful.

Reliable engineering means understanding what each result confirms—and what remains uncertain.

That was probably the most valuable lesson from this implementation.

The planned integration was completed, but several opportunities for improvement remain.

One is extending image format compatibility while maintaining safe parsing behavior.

Another is improving the ability to reproduce earlier security validations.

Different categories of evidence currently have different retention periods:

This means a report may remain available after the original files needed to reproduce its results have already been removed.

Additionally, the disposable signing materials used in an earlier historical verification were not preserved, so that exact signed execution cannot be replayed.

This revealed another important distinction:

Keeping a report is not necessarily the same as preserving everything required to reproduce it.

Evidence retention and reproducibility are related, but they are not identical.

A project may retain summary reports for weeks while no longer having access to the exact image archives or signatures used in an earlier verification.

This is something worth considering when designing CI/CD pipelines that need to support audits or repeatable investigations.

Beyond the security pipeline, future areas of exploration include service-level indicators, actionable alerts, failure recovery, and repeatable operational procedures.

These are potential improvements, not features being claimed as completed here.

Figure 4 — Evidence Retention and Reproducibility. Image archives, sanitized reports, and unsigned CI evidence have different retention periods. Preserving a report does not necessarily preserve all materials required to reproduce the original verification.

This stage of InfraPulse demonstrated that implementing security controls is only part of the challenge.

We also need to verify that those controls work with real files, handle unexpected inputs safely, and produce results that can be interpreted correctly.

But the most important lesson was understanding that a reliable system must recognize its own limits.

A green pipeline, a valid signature, or a well-structured report is not enough on its own.

We need to understand what each result actually proves.

InfraPulse continues to evolve as an open-source project focused on practical software engineering, DevOps, DevSecOps, and SRE.

GitHub: https://github.com/jacivaldocarvalho/jc-infrapulse

There are still challenges to explore, solutions to test, and lessons to share.

#9766. What is piloncillo? This sweetener makes great cookies, pan dulce, and more: Use this traditional Mexican unrefined sugar for a dash of flavor and history.

This article is part of our feature celebrating Pan Dulce. Find all things pan dulce here.

Categorically, piloncillo is a “non-centrifugal” cane sugar, meaning it is an unrefined sugar product and a true natural brown sugar. It’s mostly consumed in Mexico and Latin America, but a similar product can be found in Asia, known as jaggery in India. Though often lumped together, these unrefined dark sugars are very different from brown sugars on the market today, which have been refined to a large degree — in some cases, they’re actually just white sugar with coloring or molasses added.

Making piloncillo, on the other hand, involves an artisanal process that’s hundreds of years old. To make it, pressed cane juice is boiled to evaporate the water and deeply caramelize the sugar. The cooked cane is then poured into molds (often made of wood) and left to dry and harden. Traditional piloncillo is conical in shape and can vary in size from small to large cones but is most commonly found in a medium size that weighs about 200 grams. In Guatemala and Colombia, it is called panela, where it is cooked to a lighter degree and typically formed into a brick, rather than cone, shape. Other forms of piloncillo can be granulated or liquid (which is more rare).

Minimally processed and boldly flavored, piloncillo was historically a prized and respected foodstuff. As an unrefined cane sugar, piloncillo provides more complex vitamins and minerals than refined sugars, which undergo processing and whitening methods that also strip nutrients from the whole food. And piloncillo is also great for baking, providing notes of burnt caramel and hints of smoke. Plus, its rich molasses qualities keep baked goods moist and fresh for longer.

Always look at the ingredient label when purchasing piloncillo and make sure it says 100% pure cane juice or cane sugar. It is becoming increasingly common to find imitation products marketed as jaggery or piloncillo that contain coloring and corn syrup. You can find good piloncillo at specialty grocery stores or online at retailers.

In Mexico and throughout Latin America, piloncillo is an important ingredient in many traditional dishes. (Some will even say it’s not the “real dish” if you substitute sugar in these recipes due to the deep flavors and richness that only piloncillo can provide.) This deep, dark unrefined sugar lends its characteristic flavor and texture to popular foods and beverages such as capirotada, tepache, coyotas, atole, café de olla, calabaza al horno, coricos, and hojarascas, to name a few!

I love adding piloncillo when I’m making champurrado. In this warm and thick chocolate beverage, the piloncillo is chopped or grated and dissolved in the pot with water or milk before adding the chocolate and masa. In this recipe, the piloncillo’s intense sweet and smoky flavors pair well with the chocolate and corn masa.

While there are many dishes and uses for piloncillo, it’s not a simple substitution for granulated white sugar in recipes, but you can use it the same as you would brown sugar with a 1:1 substitution by weight.  Depending on how hard the cone is, it can be crumbled or grated for easier measuring. If it is very hard, try cutting it in half with a sharp knife and then placing it between parchment paper or a towel and beating with a rolling pin.

Find puerquitos and many more Mexican sweets in our feature celebrating pan dulce.
