#9764. Agents Are Not the Answer. Engineering Is.

How to build with rules, skills, hooks and subagents around a coding agent

For a while, I thought the problem was the model.

The agent would put a network call straight inside a screen component, and I would add a sentence to the next request: keep network calls out of the components. It would write a date-formatting helper when one already existed two folders away, and I would add another sentence. The requests got longer. The instructions file got longer. On the days the agent followed all of it, I took that as proof that the setup worked. On the days it followed none of it, I blamed the model.

It took me longer than I would like to admit to do the obvious thing, which was to stop writing and go look at what the tool was actually loading.

The rules I had written with the most care had never been read, not once. Their path patterns expected folder names that were different from the real ones. The instructions file stated a test count that was half the true number, and pointed to a document that didn't exist. In a folder above the project there was an old copy of that same file, loaded together with the new one and contradicting it. And a block I trusted completely had been letting everything through for weeks.

The model had been doing what it could with what I had put in front of it. I had been treating those files as notes to a colleague, when they were software: they had bugs, and I had never tested them.

As I write this, I don't have all the answers about how to make coding agents behave. Probably I never will. Section 9.5 lists what is still unproven, and it is not a short list. But I keep asking questions, and a few of them have turned out to be the right ones. Who decides that this piece comes into play? What happens when it fails? How would a person check?

Coding agents fail less from a lack of model capability than from a lack of engineering around the model. What the agent knows, what it can do and what stops it from making mistakes are all defined by a set of files: permanent instructions, rules per area, skills, subagents, hooks, permissions and memory. This text treats that set as software. It has an architecture, it has typical defects, and it can be tested.

The text is for anyone setting up or maintaining an environment of coding agents, in any tool. The examples use Claude Code's names, but the concepts hold for any tool that reads an instructions file such as AGENTS.md. Section 9 shows all of it applied to a real financial platform, with measured numbers. That is where the story in the prologue comes from.

A coding agent is a language model running in a loop: it reads the request, decides on an action (read a file, run a command, edit), receives the result, and decides on the next one. Everything it knows at that moment is in the context window: the system instructions, the configuration files that were loaded, the conversation, and the tool results. The model has no memory other than what is there and what it learned in training.

There is a useful image for this, attributed to Andrej Karpathy: the model is the processor and the context window is the RAM. Context engineering is deciding what occupies that memory at each step.

Intuition says that giving the model more information helps. It is a reasonable intuition. It is also wrong, or at least wrong past a certain point.

Anthropic describes the phenomenon as context rot: as the window fills up, the model gets worse at retrieving each individual piece of information. Attention is a budget. An important rule buried in a thousand lines of instructions has less effect than the same rule in a file of a hundred.

The practical consequence is the central principle of this text: look for the smallest set of high-signal tokens that produces the behavior you want. Every piece described from here on is a way of applying that principle.

The files that configure an agent have readers (the models). They have behavior (what the agents do because of them). They have bugs (a hook that doesn't fire, a path pattern that doesn't match). And they have debt (a number that stopped being true).

In other words, the practices that apply to product code apply to them as well: one responsibility per file, clear names, nothing duplicated, tests, review and maintenance.

This is the text loaded in every session, for every agent. It holds what is always true: what the project is, the vocabulary of the domain, the real commands, the security rules, the forbidden zones and the definition of done.

Because it enters every context, each line costs attention on every task. The rules for writing it:

A wrong fact in this file costs more than a missing one, because it teaches the model to act with confidence on something false.

Rules are the instructions file sliced by responsibility: one rule for the backend, another for the app, another for tests. A rule can declare which paths it applies to; in that case it is only loaded when a file from that area enters the conversation. A rule with no scope is always loaded, like the main file.

Rules are binding. Write "every new route has an entry in the permissions manifest", not "consider adding one". And name model files: pointing to a well-made file of 44 lines teaches more than describing what a clean route is.

A skill is a folder with an instructions file that has a name and a description. Of all the skills available, the model sees only those two things: name and description. When the task matches a description, it loads the body. This is called progressive disclosure. The knowledge exists, but it only takes up context when it is needed.

That is why the description is the most important part of a skill. It has to say what the skill covers and when to use it, in the words that show up in real requests. A vague description never fires.

Skills hold recipes (how to create a migration), formats (the body of a pull request), catalogs (code smells and their refactorings) and technology knowledge written from the project's real code. A skill can also be invoked by hand, like a command, and can be marked so the model never starts it on its own. That is useful for expensive flows.

A subagent is a role defined in a file: description, allowed tools, model and a system text. When it is called, it runs in a new, empty context window. It receives only the brief the calling agent wrote and the project's instructions files. When it finishes, it hands back a report. Everything it read along the way is thrown out.

The cost is real: the subagent knows nothing about the conversation, and what comes back is a summary. Detail is lost in both directions. Delegating only pays off when the work is large, independent, or needs fresh eyes.

Hooks are scripts the tool executes on events: before a tool call, after it, at the end of a turn. A hook that runs before the call can allow it, deny it or ask for confirmation. A hook that runs after can return text that enters the agent's context.

Hooks are the only piece that doesn't depend on the model obeying. They have two uses:

Rules for hooks: minimal dependencies, errors never silenced, denial messages that say what to do instead, fast execution, and tests with expected allow and deny cases.

Keep that list in mind. Each item on it was learned from something that went wrong, and we will get to those in section 9.3.

Declarative lists of deny, ask and allow, by tool pattern and path pattern. They cover the simple case with no script: never read secret files, always ask before a commit. Whatever needs logic (block an existing migration, allow a new one) goes into a hook.

A directory where the agent writes down facts that should outlive the session: decisions made and the reasons for them, the preferences of whoever works with it, facts about the environment that aren't in the repository. A short index is loaded at the start of each session.

Memory is not a diary. Task state and summaries of finished work stay out, because they age fast and take up context forever.

The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for exposing external tools and data (ticket manager, database, documents) to the agent through a typed interface. It replaces hand-made integrations. Every connected server adds tool descriptions to the context, so the same discipline applies: connect what gets used.

When the description matches, or by command

Birgitta Böckeler, in Context Engineering for Coding Agents, organizes these pieces around one question: who decides that the piece comes into play?

There is a detail here that is easy to miss. Even when loading is guaranteed, obedience is not. A rule in the instructions file is always in the context, and the model can still fail to follow it in a long task. Only hooks and permissions guarantee the effect.

Out of this comes what I consider the most useful design rule in this text:

can be checked by a tool (types, lint, tests)

requires judgment and applies to one kind of task

requires focus, a different permission or fresh eyes

When an agent gets something wrong, the right question is which layer was missing. The fix goes into that layer. One more sentence in the next request fixes nothing.

In Building effective agents, Anthropic recommends starting with the simplest solution and using composed, predictable patterns before handing out open-ended autonomy. There are five patterns:

One design that works well is to have a single agent the person talks to. It answers questions by reading the code, gives opinions, and delegates when the work calls for it. This agent runs as the main session, not as a subagent, and it has the list of specialists it can call.

Three rules keep this design cheap and safe:

The subagent knows only the brief. Nothing else.

Anthropic reports, in How we built our multi-agent research system, that vague briefs made subagents duplicate work, leave gaps or misread the task. A complete brief has:

The report has a fixed format. For a critic: verdict, blocking points, warnings and suggestions, each with file and line. For a builder: files changed, what was removed, commands run and their results, and what could not be done. The fixed format is what makes the flow auditable.

Before calling review, it checks the acceptance criteria in the code itself, runs the verification commands, compares the error counts against the baseline, and goes through the list of changed files looking for anything out of scope. When something fails, the work goes back to the responsible agent with the concrete problem. The limit is three rounds. After that the flow stops and reports.

Systems with several agents spend several times more tokens than a simple conversation. The same Anthropic text reports prototypes that created dozens of subagents for trivial questions.

Orchestration pays for itself on high-value tasks, with independent parts or parts that need separate review. For a one-line fix, it is waste.

The term comes from Kent Beck and was spread by Martin Fowler in Refactoring. A smell is a surface sign of a deeper structural problem. It isn't a bug: the code works. The cost shows up later, when every change gets more expensive and riskier.

The most used catalog groups smells into five families:

Long function, giant file, long parameter list, primitive obsession

Repeated if chain by type, forced inheritance

Duplicated code, a change that requires editing many files

One change becomes ten, and one gets forgotten

Dead code, abstraction for a future that never arrived, a comment that explains confusing code

Skipped layers, a function that lives off another module's data, long access chains

None of these causes is solved by asking the agent to "write clean code". Each one calls for a different piece.

Before writing: show what good looks like and what already exists.

Numeric limits work better than adjectives: a target of 40 lines per function, new files under 400, at most 4 parameters, at most 3 levels of nesting. The layering rule says where each kind of logic lives, which keeps the handler or the screen from accumulating everything.

Right after writing: deterministic feedback.

A hook that runs after each write analyzes the file and returns a list of problems to the agent, with the instruction to fix them or justify them in the report. Ideally this hook runs the project's linter. Where there is no linter, pattern searches cover part of the ground: too many parameters, deep nesting, an empty catch, commented-out code, too much state in one component. This check is approximate and has to be treated that way. It is a warning, not proof.

Before reporting, the builder runs a short self-check on its own diff. Did any function go over the limit? Did I write a block that already existed, and where did I look? Did I add a literal with business meaning? Did any handler or screen gain data access, an HTTP call or a formula? Did I leave anything dead?

In review: fresh eyes and bounded cleanup.

Every task leaves the area it touched cleaner than it found it.

The limit is what makes the rule workable: the cleanup stays inside the files and functions the task already touches, and it is smaller than the task itself. A cleanup bigger than the feature is another task. Without that limit, the agent turns a small fix into a refactoring nobody asked for and nobody can review.

Known security problems stay outside this rule. Fixing them as a side effect of another task mixes together changes that need their own review.

Small functions, names that say what the thing is

Deep modules: simple interface, hidden complexity

A Philosophy of Software Design (Ousterhout)

Thin route with a tested core; subagent with a short description and a fixed report

Characterization tests before touching legacy code

Working Effectively with Legacy Code (Feathers)

First step of the recipe for decomposing large files

Fitness functions: automatic checks of architectural characteristics

Building Evolutionary Architectures (Ford, Parsons and Kua)

The study Configuration Smells in AGENTS.md Files (arXiv 2606.15828) put together the first catalog of these defects from 100 open source repositories with AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md files. According to coverage of the study, at least one defect showed up in 91 of the 100 files, and the three most frequent were:

The study also observes that these defects tend to show up together, and in the company of conflicting instructions.

Putting that catalog together with practice, the checklist looks like this:

"Don't use any", "no console.log" in prose

Configure the linter and run it in a hook or in CI

Count the always-loaded lines, adding up all files

Move recipes to skills and areas to scoped rules

PR format, migration steps in the global file

Ask of each section: does this apply to every task?

Extract into a skill with a precise description

List every instructions file the tool loads, including folders above

A version, count or path that doesn't match the code

Compare against the repository; every measurement has a date

The rule lives in one place and is referenced

Its tools can't be restricted and its trigger can't be described

All the knowledge inside the agent's text

Of the ten, the false guarantee is the one I would single out, because it is the most dangerous. A block that fails in silence gives everyone the feeling of protection. Hooks need tests for the same reason authorization code does.

The most repeated recommendation for coding agents is to give the model a verifiable target. Without one, the agent optimizes for looking right. In order of return:

Measuring the flow closes the loop: how many tasks needed more than one round of correction, which categories of defect the reviewer finds most, how much a task costs. Those numbers say which rule, skill or hook is missing.

A regulated platform for online medical appointments and prescriptions, with two repositories: a TypeScript backend of about 175 thousand lines and a mobile app of about 113 thousand.

An audit was carried out by four agents in parallel, with evidence by file and line. This is what it measured:

The audit's conclusion was about process, not knowledge. The model files proved that the team knew how to do it well. Every new feature had been copied from its nearest neighbor, and nothing stood in the way of that.

It is exactly the condition in which a coding agent makes the problem worse.

The dosage checker doesn't read the code in order to give an opinion. It recalculates the doses independently, with mandatory scenarios, and compares.

This is the part of the case I find most useful, and it is the part that looked worst at the time. There were six mistakes.

Hooks that didn't protect. This is the block from the prologue that let everything through. The original hooks called an interpreter that didn't exist on the machine. The error was silenced, the script exited with success, and everything was allowed. Migration protection did not exist for weeks, and nobody noticed. Lesson: minimal dependencies, errors never swallowed, tests for the hook.

Rules that never loaded. The path patterns expected folder names different from the real ones. The rules were there, written with care, and were not read a single time. Lesson: test the pattern against a real path.

Wrong facts in the instructions file. An outdated framework version, a test count at half the real number, a reference to a document that didn't exist. Lesson: measure and date.

A hook that blocked legitimate work. The pattern looked for the text of a forbidden command anywhere on the line, and it matched a file that merely mentioned the command. Lesson: analyze the structure of the command, not the loose text.

Conflicting instructions. When the checklist from section 6 was applied to the configuration itself, an old copy of the instructions file turned up in a folder above, loaded together with the current one and contradicting it. Lesson: list everything the tool loads, not just what is in the project folder.

Style rules in prose. The backend had no linter, so "no any, no debug logging, no fixed decimal places" went into the text and into a pattern-search hook. This is Lint Leakage, accepted knowingly as a provisional measure. The definitive fix is the linter.

Before this work, the repository had a configuration that looked like protection. Now it has one that has been tested.

This changes the conditions under which code gets written there. The audit in section 9.1 found components of 6 thousand lines because every new feature was copied from its nearest neighbor and nothing stood in the way. Today an agent working in that repository starts from the model files. It receives the map of what already exists before writing its first line. It hears about a function that passed the limit in time to fix it. And it cannot grow the files that were marked as never to grow.

The copying that produced the old code has been cut off at each of the four points from section 5.

Three things come next, in this order: the linter on the backend, CI blocking the merge, and the evaluations of the flow. With them, the same baselines that today say where the code stands will say, task after task, how far it has moved

Order of adoption, from the strongest guarantee to the weakest:

Before creating any new piece, eight questions:

Which layer? Permanent fact, on-demand recipe, isolated role or guarantee?

Does something already cover this? Extend it or reference it.

What is the exact trigger? Test it against a real case.

What are the minimum tools? Who writes and who only reads?

What is the output? A fixed format, with evidence by file and line.

How does a person verify it? Command, baseline, diff.

What happens when it fails? A message that teaches the alternative; a limit on rounds.

What is the date of the measurement, and who maintains it?

There is a scene in Neon Genesis Evangelion that I kept coming back t

For most of the series, everyone treats the Evangelions as giant robots. They have pilots, hangars, launch rails and a maintenance crew. Then one of them tears off its own plating in the middle of a fight, and the head scientist, Ritsuko Akagi, says what the engineers had known all along. The plates were never armor. They are restraints, put there to hold back something that is alive, far stronger than the people who built it, and not fully understood by any of them.

I think this is the most accurate picture I have of what this text describes.

The Eva is not a robot. Nobody at NERV programmed it line by line. They found a way to work with it, and then built everything else around that fact: the plating, the cockpit, the cables, the command room. A language model is in the same position. The engineering in sections 2 to 8 is the plating and the command room.

The cable decides how the fight goes. An Eva runs on an external power cable. When the cable is cut, the internal battery lasts five minutes, and every plan made in the command room starts from that number. That is the context window from section 1. It is the scarce resource, and the design is done around it.

Synchronization is a request. The pilot doesn't steer with levers. The pilot thinks, and the Eva moves, as long as the two are in sync. Some days the sync is high and the machine does exactly what was intended. Some days it barely moves. And a few times it stops listening altogether and acts on its own. That is an instruction: followed most of the time, with no promise about the rest.

The restraints are the guarantee. What NERV could not afford to leave to synchronization, it bolted on. The plating doesn't depend on the pilot being calm or on the Eva agreeing. That is a hook. And the series shows what a restraint that fails looks like, which is the false guarantee from section 6: until the moment it breaks, it looks exactly the same as one that works.

Three computers, one decision. NERV's decisions go through the MAGI, three supercomputers that each hold a different side of the same mind and vote. They exist because a single opinion, however intelligent, inherits its own bias. That is the reviewer from section 2.4, who never saw the implementer's reasoning.

Taking the pilot out is the worst idea in the story. At one point the command decides the pilot is hesitating too much and switches to an autopilot, the Dummy Plug. The Eva finishes the job, and what it does cannot be undone, while the pilot sits inside screaming for it to stop. Section 8 is there for that reason: commit, push, migration and publishing stay with the person.

And when it works, everyone is in it. The operation I like most in the series is the one in which the electricity of the entire country is routed into a single rifle. There is a pilot who shoots and a pilot who holds the shield, engineers on the transformers, operators calling out numbers, a commander who has made the plan, and the three computers giving the odds. The first shot misses. The second one doesn't. It is orchestration, including the cost: you black out a country to stop an Angel, not to fix one line.

What I believe will outlast the tools is the question NERV's engineers had to answer for every part of that machine. Is this something we ask of the pilot, or is this something we bolt on?

Martin Fowler and Kent Beck, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code.

Robert C. Martin, Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship.

John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design.

Michael Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code.

Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons and Patrick Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

#9761. How do you architect robust Playwright E2E tests to validate coordinated UI state consistency across multiple, interconn

Posted on Nov 16 • Originally published at styrow.dev

🔥 Playwright Alert: Is your SPA's UI consistency causing flaky E2E tests?

⚠️ 90% of engineers struggle to reliably validate complex, coordinated UI state across multiple components in Playwright. Here's how to master it.

In sophisticated Single-Page Applications (SPAs), especially dashboards, user actions or backend pushes trigger cascaded, asynchronous UI updates across interconnected components. Traditional Playwright assertions, focused on individual elements, often lead to flakiness due to race conditions or partial updates. The real challenge is verifying the entire coordinated state is consistent and stable, not just isolated elements.

❌ Relying on page.waitForTimeout() or isolated assertions makes tests brittle. ❌ Missing the "collective harmony" of components leads to false passes or failures.

To architect robust Playwright E2E tests for coordinated UI states, embrace holistic state definition, event-driven waiting, and comprehensive validation.

Here’s how to implement this using page.waitForFunction for true stability:

✅ Define a holistic stable state for your UI. ✅ Use page.waitForFunction to wait for all components to reach that stable state. ✅ Avoid arbitrary waitForTimeout() – wait for explicit signals. ✅ Assert the collective state of interconnected components, not just isolated elements.

Q: Why are traditional Playwright assertions often flaky in complex SPAs? A: They don't account for asynchronous, cascaded updates, leading to assertions on temporary or inconsistent states.

Q: What is the most robust way to wait for UI stability across multiple components? A: Use page.waitForFunction() with a custom JavaScript function that checks for multiple, holistic stability conditions (e.g., absence of all loaders, presence of specific data across elements).

#9759. How to Prevent Silent Failures in Multi-Agent AI Systems

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

Orbit is my multi-agent content system. A planner directs each run, and a Bash orchestrator runs the agents in sequence or in parallel. Most of the interesting problems in it are about what the agents write. This one was about what an agent returned.

On 24 March 2026 the analytics agent returned placeholder code instead of data. Nothing crashed. The output file existed, the next agent read it, and the system carried on for five cycles.

That is the failure I now design for first. An agent that errors is easy to see: something exits with a failure and the run stops. An agent that returns something plausible but wrong is quiet, and every step after it treats the wrong thing as input.

The fix was output validation after every agent run, in the orchestrator itself. It asks three questions of each output:

None of these are clever. They are the checks a person would make on opening the file. The difference is that the orchestrator makes them every time, so one agent's output only becomes the next agent's input once it has passed.

Validation on its own turns a quiet failure into a loud one. That is better, but a run that halts is still a missed run. So the critical agents (analytics, scriptwriter, editor and researcher) get one retry, with an explicit instruction appended to the prompt, and the run halts only if the retry also fails.

Two ideas sit inside that rule. Criticality belongs to the agent, not to the failure: Orbit has agent criticality tiers, and the halt applies to the critical ones. And the retry is not the same call made twice. It tells the model what the output has to be, which gives a near miss a real chance to become a pass.

In May 2026 I fixed the next layer of the same problem. Some of Orbit's agents run on local models through Ollama. When a local model failed, the orchestrator restored that agent's last-good snapshot so the run could continue. A sensible fallback, except that nothing checked the snapshot. A last-good file that was not actually good would be copied straight back in.

So recovery now goes through the same kind of gate as a fresh run:

The second point matters more than it looks. A green health check that hides a fallback teaches you to stop reading the health check. Marking a recovery as a concern keeps the dashboard honest: the run finished, but something needed rescuing, and I want to see that.

None of this needs a framework. The checks are a few lines of Python inside the Bash orchestrator. What it needs is the habit of asking, at every boundary, what a plausible wrong answer would look like, and refusing to pass it on.

#9756. When I tell Cursor "just make it work", this rule stops the shortcut from rotting

Cursor is very obedient about the word "quick."

If I say "just make it work," it will often make something work by skipping the parts that are annoying: the ownership check, the empty state, the test, the rollback. The feature looks done. A week later I cannot remember which of those shortcuts is load-bearing, and one of them is in a path real users hit.

I got tired of cleaning that up, so I stopped treating "MVP" as a quality setting. I treat it as a scope setting. The rule lives in .cursor/rules/ and I pull it in when I hear myself say "hack this in," "just for now," or "we'll tidy it later."

The useful question is not "how do we write this faster?" It is "what can we not build yet?"

I also tell it what it is not allowed to cut, even in a hurry:

That split is the whole point. "Quick" means the settings UI can wait. It does not mean the webhook can be processed twice.

Some debt is still worth taking. When I take it, I want to find it again on a Monday morning, not rediscover it in production.

This is boring on purpose. The alternative is a vague "we'll refactor this" that nobody can search for.

If I say "prototype" or "throwaway," I want it in /sandbox or on a separate branch, and I want the agent to say out loud that it is not production-safe.

If a real user can reach it, it is production. The "never cut" list applies. Putting a prototype in the same routes as checkout, "just to see," is how a labelled shortcut becomes an unlabelled incident.

Save this as .cursor/rules/60-mvp-not-sloppy.mdc. It is not always-on. It should attach when the task is a prototype, a spike, or a deliberately small first version.

After that I still ask for a short done-summary: what changed, how to verify, and which DEBT(solo) items were added. If the summary has no debt list and the diff quietly skipped a test, the rule did not run.

This is not a substitute for a small-diff rule, a bug-fix playbook, or a real review. It only answers one failure mode: the agent heard "hurry" and lowered the quality bar instead of the feature bar.

If you want the rest of the set I use (core working agreement, feature slicing, root-cause bug fixes, PR review, landing copy), I bundled them as a one-time Cursor pack: shipstack.sognia.workers.dev/cursor-pack. The rule above is usable on its own.

#9754. One Query, Six Ranked Lists, One Answer: Tuning Rank Fusion for Multilingual Search

Posted on Nov 16 • Originally published at Medium

How one constant in Reciprocal Rank Fusion lets a confident top match stand out — and why the right value depends on how correlated your retrievers are.

When you type a query into SpotRecall, my private on-device browser recall extension, it does not run one search. It runs six.

The query is first searched as typed. Then Chrome's on-device Translator turns it into the other two languages SpotRecall covers — English, Japanese, and Chinese — because, as I wrote earlier in this series, translating the query beats shipping a model four times larger. Each of those three variants is searched twice: once by BM25 keyword search and once by a small multilingual embedding model (multilingual-e5-small, int8, running locally).

Three variants times two retrievers gives six ranked lists. The user sees one result page.

Version 1.3.1 is about the step in between: how those six lists become one ordering, and how to make the page you are actually looking for land at the top. Measured on 54 real queries against a 1088-page personal history, the full set of changes in this release brings mean reciprocal rank (MRR) to 0.828. This post covers the fusion stage at the center of it.

SpotRecall merges its lists with weighted Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), the standard technique for hybrid search. Every document receives, from every list it appears in, a contribution based only on its rank:

RRF is popular for good reasons. It needs no score calibration between retrievers — a BM25 score and a cosine similarity live on unrelated scales, but ranks are always comparable. It is a few lines of code. And it rewards agreement: a page that several retrievers like rises.

k sets how steeply the reward falls with rank. In other words, it decides how much a confident first place is worth compared with a place further down the list.

The value you see in tutorials and libraries is k = 60, from the original RRF paper. Here is what it does to a single list (ranks start at 1):

With k = 60 the curve is almost flat: being first is barely better than being twentieth. That shifts the weight of the decision onto how many lists a page appears in.

A worked example makes the difference concrete. Take a page that is the clear first result of one list, and another page that sits at rank 10 in three lists (unweighted, for simplicity):

Neither answer is universally right. It depends on what agreement between lists means.

k = 60 was designed for fusing many independent systems — different engines, different models, different teams. When independent systems agree on a document, that agreement is strong evidence, and a flat curve that rewards it makes sense.

SpotRecall's six lists are not independent. A query and its translation describe the same intent; their embeddings sit close together; BM25 over a Japanese translation and BM25 over the Chinese one often retrieve overlapping pages. When correlated lists agree, they are largely repeating one opinion.

So for this pipeline, a steeper curve fits better. k = 3 lets a strong first place in one list compete on equal terms with moderate agreement across several, which matches what a user means by "the page I was looking for."

The second piece concerns the embedding retriever. Nearest-neighbour search always returns the number of results you ask for. It never says "nothing here is really similar."

With e5-small, cosine similarities for real pages cluster in a narrow band, roughly 0.75 to 0.9. The top few hits of a vector list are usually meaningful; by rank 18 the score difference from rank 3 can be tiny, and the content often is not related.

1.3.1 therefore keeps only vector hits within a fixed margin of the best one:

When the model is confident, several close matches pass. When one page stands out, the list becomes short and decisive. Either way, the vector retriever contributes what it is sure about, and BM25 handles the rest.

The whole stage is a small pure function, shared by the extension and the offline evaluation so that tuning measures exactly what ships:

Each behaviour is pinned by a test. For example, when the original query and a translation each produce a page at the same rank, the original's page must come first; and a weak vector hit (0.7 next to a 0.9) must not reach the fused list at all.

All of these numbers were tuned against 54 labeled queries — Chinese, Japanese, English, and cross-lingual — replayed offline against a real 1088-record backup, with the offline ranking verified to be identical to the live extension.

With so few queries, it is easy to find parameters that fit them perfectly and help nobody else. A grid search proposed other values. When I tuned on half of the queries and tested on the other half, those values did not beat the shipped ones, so they did not ship. The values above are the ones that kept their gains on held-out queries.

For reference, an early configuration with textbook k = 60, equal weights, and untrimmed vector lists scored around 0.30 MRR on the first 32 queries. After this release, the full 54-query set sits at 0.828, and the worst-case configuration (simulating bookmark-heavy profiles) at 0.826. Those two figures are not on the same query set, so read them as direction rather than a precise delta. The next posts cover the other contributors and the evaluation loop in detail.

Rank fusion constants are not magic numbers. They encode an assumption about your retrievers: how independent they are, and how much a confident first place should be worth.

If your hybrid search fuses a keyword list, a vector list, and a few query rewrites, those lists are probably correlated. Measure k rather than copying 60 — and give each retriever the chance to contribute only what it is genuinely confident about.

The honest caveat: k = 3 is right for this pipeline — few lists, strongly correlated, a personal corpus of about a thousand pages. The general advice is to measure, not to use 3.

SpotRecall is open source under AGPL-3.0. spotrecall.com · source on GitHub · install from the Chrome Web Store.

This is Post 11 in Building SpotRecall, and the first post in Season 3: sharper, measured search.

#9752. How Mitts Makes Parallel Rust Builds Faster Than Cargo

Systems engineer: distributed systems, low-latency market data, trading infrastructure, AI runtimes & search. C++, Rust, Go, Python.

Systems engineer: distributed systems, low-latency market data, trading infrastructure, AI runtimes & search. C++, Rust, Go, Python.

Systems engineer: distributed systems, low-latency market data, trading infrastructure, AI runtimes & search. C++, Rust, Go, Python.

Cargo takes minutes. Mitts takes seconds.

For parallel work, the question is simple: when will the whole batch of builds be ready? The code is already split across branches. Now you need completed artifacts to move on to verification.

In The Hundred, twelve rustls worktrees on Linux x86_64 took 3 min 42 s with Cargo. With Mitts, 9.3 s. That is the completion time of the whole batch for one project, not a corpus total or the time of the first worktree to finish.

Figure 1. One heavy project from the study; medians of three repeats. Shared caches were prewarmed, local targets were empty. Priming time is excluded; the axis starts at zero.

Plain Cargo in this configuration has no shared compilation cache between worktrees: each fresh checkout starts with an empty target directory. Mitts and sccache receive prewarmed shared caches. Sccache starts warm too, yet finishes this batch in 3 min 59 s: caching work inside compiler calls does not remove the entire repeated build process.

I chose a long-build example to make the wait for artifacts concrete. It does not promise the same time for every project or measure how fast an agent completes its entire task.

An agent gets a worktree. A reviewer gets another. A fix gets a third. Each has its own target/. Source isolation is clean. But another checkout should not automatically mean repeating identical, reusable compilation work.

“Give each agent its own target directory” is an isolation policy with a compilation bill attached. I built Mitts to keep the worktrees separate while letting them share completed work.

The main scenario builds tests with test --no-run in twelve worktrees of one project, spread across four commits, starting together. It compares plain Cargo, Cargo with sccache, and Mitts on the same machine and toolchain. Cargo runs offline. Test execution is outside the timed build.

Every repeat uses fresh worktrees with empty local target/ directories and pre-fetched sources. The shared caches start from snapshots primed by one untimed build of the first commit. The timed swarm measures reuse across those fresh checkouts and compilation of the differences at the other commits; it does not include that initial priming cost.

The study selects 100 open-source Rust projects. The measured count is 100 on macOS, 90 on Linux x86_64, and 100 on Linux aarch64. The machines have 24, 32, and 128 logical CPUs respectively. The corpus and full public machine specifications are on the study page.

Each reading is the median of three repeats. The rustls chart shows one project; the full corpus exposes the distribution. Duration labels are truncated to the displayed precision, while bar lengths use the underlying values.

All measured projects remain in the results, including seven Linux x86_64 runs marked “wide spread.” An idle gate checked CPU load and foreign compiler activity; it did not remove the resident agent sessions on the Mac. Three repeats are not a confidence interval, and totals give heavy projects more influence. The study’s project tables and reduced data expose that distribution.

Rustls above is one heavy project on Linux x86_64. Now look at the full Mac corpus to see which repeated work can be removed:

Sccache clearly helps CPU time. But in this workload it still starts a wrapper for each compiler invocation, Cargo still plans each build and runs build scripts, and linking outputs such as test binaries are outside sccache’s compilation cache. Cutting compiler work inside those calls does not remove the entire repeated build process.

Consider actix-web on the Mac: the twelve-worktree build took 5 min 22 s with Cargo, 5 min 23 s with sccache, and 56 s with Mitts. Cargo made 3,408 compiler invocations; Mitts made 181.

Disk also needs two definitions. Device bytes written measure writes reaching the block device. du measures the workspace files and shared store, counting each copy-on-write clone in full on XFS. On Linux x86_64 (XFS), disk-in-use totals fell from 641 GB to 484 GB, while device writes fell from 651 GB to 106 GB. Those readings describe different costs; neither can substitute for the other.

The obvious shortcut is a shared CARGO_TARGET_DIR. It also shares mutable outputs.

The study deliberately puts a failing test into worktree twelve. All worktrees must compile and produce the same test-binary counts as plain Cargo. Untimed smoke checks then require the modified worktree to fail on that test while a clean worktree passes.

The shared-target demonstration failed that check: the injected failure was missed or leaked into a clean worktree. It was excluded from the scores.

Great: a quicker build, followed by a test from the wrong checkout. I wanted a build I could use.

That result concerns concurrent builds at different commits, and it demands more than “the directories are now the same” when designing reuse between agents.

Mitts reads the existing Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock, plans the compilation graph, and invokes rustc directly. The technical documentation describes six phases: resolve, fetch, plan, key, execute, publish.

Each unit receives an action key derived from its toolchain, target, profile, flags, features, source content, dependency action keys, and tracked environment. Matching inputs can reuse an existing result. A changed input changes the key. An input Mitts cannot account for makes the unit uncached or explicitly unsupported.

Figure 2. One unit of work. Identical tracked inputs can share a result; changed inputs receive a different key. Worktrees and their output directories remain separate.

The important boundary is between an immutable store and a workspace’s mutable output view. Objects are hashed when published, staged, made read-only, and atomically renamed into the store. The action-cache entry is written last. Restoring uses a filesystem reflink, a read-only hardlink, or a copy; a workspace never receives a writable alias to a shared object.

Restore does not re-hash every object by default. It trusts the atomically published, read-only objects. MITTS_VERIFY_RESTORE=1 opts into checking every object’s hash before restoration. That distinction matters when explaining both the trust model and the work a cache hit performs.

Cross-worktree reuse also requires path independence. Qualifying workspace units use remapped paths; units with a custom build script, compile-time CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR, a declared impure proc-macro dependency, or paths outside the workspace root retain checkout-specific keys. Mitts additionally checks artifacts for the workspace path before publishing them under a path-independent key. Reuse is conditional, not an assumption that two crates with the same name are interchangeable.

On a cache hit, the result is restored immediately, without a per-key lock. On a miss, builds cooperate through that lock and re-check the cache after acquiring it. If another build is producing a needed unit, a worker can process other ready units and return later. A machine-wide jobserver bounds compiler concurrency across Mitts processes. Build-script outputs and declared inputs are tracked too, but staging is not an OS sandbox: undeclared file reads remain the author’s responsibility.

The useful abstraction is completed work with a known identity. Each agent keeps its own checkout; identical eligible work does not need another compiler run merely because its consumer lives in another directory.

One cold build. Plain Cargo finished first on 71 of 100 Mac projects, 60 of 90 Linux x86_64 projects, and 77 of 100 Linux aarch64 projects; the Mac also had one exact tie. On the Mac, Cargo’s advantage reached 6.2 s for procs. Against cold sccache, Mitts finished first on 86 of 100, 90 of 90, and 98 of 100 respectively. An empty store has nothing to reuse, while Mitts must hash inputs and populate it; plain Cargo is a strong choice for that workload.

Edit one file. Mitts finished before Cargo on 49 of 71, 43 of 64, and 42 of 71 projects, in the same machine order. Cargo won the remainder. Its intra-crate incremental compilation can be cheaper than rebuilding a large crate as a whole unit. The smaller denominators matter: some edit probes failed to compile under all three tools, including crates that deny missing documentation.

Replay ten commits in one directory. Mitts finished first on 58 of 100, 63 of 90, and 52 of 99 projects. Yet the independently computed per-tool medians were close: Cargo/Mitts 5.6/5.7 s, 3.5/3.6 s, and 9.0/9.1 s. More project wins do not necessarily produce a lower overall median.

Peak memory of one compiler process. Mitts invokes the same rustc; an individual compiler or linker still needs essentially the same working memory. The CPU and disk savings above are not a claim that one compiler suddenly becomes small.

Mitts is pre-release software for Linux and macOS. Windows, cross-compilation beyond the host target, and a remote or team cache are not supported yet. Undeclared build-script and proc-macro inputs need care. A machine-wide store helps cooperating builds on that machine; it is not an organization-wide cache service.

If your day is one checkout and small edits inside a large crate, the incremental-build results deserve your attention. If your day is agents, worktrees, branch switches, and review builds repeating the same eligible inputs, the reuse results address your workload directly.

Start with the installation and usage documentation and inspect the full study. Mitts uses ordinary Cargo manifests; mitts explain shows its plan and action keys without compiling.

Keep source isolation. Keep correctness checks. But stop treating duplicate compilation as the unavoidable price of giving another agent a worktree.

When AI Coding Agents Start Acting Like Tech Leads

Systems engineer: distributed systems, low-latency market data, trading infrastructure, AI runtimes & search. C++, Rust, Go, Python.

#9749. 국내 대표 AI 기업 11개사, 2026년 허깅페이스 공개 모델 다운로드 분석

Posted on Nov 16 • Originally published at livegpt.tistory.com

요약: 2026년 국내 AI 기업 11개사가 허깅페이스에 공개한 언어모델 174개의 다운로드를 분석했다. 직전 30일 136만 회 중 82.2%, 올해 누적 666만 회 중 58.0%가 비드래프트 모델이고, 30일 상위 5개 모델은 모두 GGUF·NVFP4 압축 형태다.

올해 국내 AI 기업들은 앞다퉈 자체 모델을 허깅페이스에 공개했다. 세계 개발자들은 그중 어떤 모델을 실제로 내려받았을까. 2026년 1월 1일 이후 공개된 모델만 놓고, 국내 대표 AI 기업 11개사의 다운로드를 직전 30일과 올해 누적으로 나눠 분석했다.

분석 대상은 LG AI연구원, SK텔레콤, 업스테이지, 모티프테크놀로지스, 비드래프트, 네이버, 카카오, 엔씨소프트(NC AI), KT, 크래프톤, 트릴리온랩스의 공식 허깅페이스 계정이다. 기준은 하나다. 개발사가 자기 공식 계정으로 직접 공개한 언어모델만 센다. 다른 개발사 모델을 원래 이름 그대로 다시 올린 변환본과 해외·개인 재배포본은 넣지 않았고, 이 규칙은 모든 회사에 똑같이 적용했다. 수치는 2026년 11월 16일 허깅페이스 공개 API 실측값이며, 글로벌 LLM 다운로드 리더보드 한국 탭의 「11개사 2026 분석」, 「2026년 출시」 보기에서 같은 숫자를 매일 확인할 수 있다.

허핀달·허시먼 지수(HHI)는 회사별 점유율(%)을 제곱해 더한 값으로, 0에 가까울수록 고르게 나뉘고 10,000이면 한 회사가 전부 가진다. 미국 법무부 합병 지침(2023)은 1,800을 넘으면 고집중 시장으로 본다. 2026년 국산 공개 모델 다운로드는 30일 기준 6,842, 누적 기준 4,298로 두 기준 모두 이 선을 크게 넘는다. 다운로드가 소수의 회사, 그리고 그 안에서도 소수의 모델에 강하게 몰려 있다는 뜻이다. 상위 5개 모델이 11개사 전체 30일 다운로드의 89.5%를 차지한다.

두 기준 모두 비드래프트가 1위다. 30일 1,119,177회(82.2%), 누적 3,862,798회(58.0%)다. 2위부터는 그림이 갈린다. 누적에서는 LG AI연구원이 1,970,599회(29.6%)로 2위다. 4월에 공개한 엑사원 4.5가 한 해 동안 쌓은 결과다. 직전 30일 기준으로는 SK텔레콤(86,439회)과 크래프톤(65,700회)이 2·3위로 올라선다. 크래프톤은 10월 말 첫 언어모델 Raon-1을 공개한 지 한 달 만에 이 자리에 들어왔다. 엔씨소프트와 KT는 올해 허깅페이스에 새 언어모델을 공개하지 않았다.

직전 30일 상위 다섯 모델은 하나도 빠짐없이 GGUF나 NVFP4 같은 압축(양자화) 형태로 공개된 모델이다. 2026년 공개 국산 모델 상위 30개로 넓히면, 30일 다운로드의 92.8%가 압축 형태에서 나왔다(GGUF 85.7%, NVFP4 6.4%, 기타 압축 0.8%, 원본 7.2%). 개발자가 원하는 것은 원본 가중치를 받아 직접 변환하는 수고가 아니라, 내려받자마자 자기 노트북이나 서버에서 돌릴 수 있는 파일이다. 국산 모델 다운로드 경쟁의 승부처는 「어떤 모델을 만드느냐」에서 「어떤 형태로 내놓느냐」로 옮겨 가고 있다.

크기도 눈여겨볼 만하다. 30일 1위는 1,800억 개 매개변수의 POCKET-Darwin-180B이고, 4위는 3,535억 개 매개변수의 SK텔레콤 A.X-K2(NVFP4)다. 작은 모델일수록 많이 받힐 것이라는 통념과 달리, 거대 모델을 가볍게 압축해 개인 장비에서 돌리려는 수요가 크다는 점이 숫자로 드러난다.

누적 다운로드는 일찍 공개할수록 유리하다. 그래서 공개 후 경과일로 나눈 하루 평균과 최근 30일 하루 평균을 함께 보면 모델의 흐름이 드러난다.

엑사원 4.5는 공개 직후 다운로드가 크게 몰린 뒤 안정 구간에 들어선 모델이다. 반면 POCKET-Darwin-180B는 최근 30일 하루 평균이 공개 후 평균보다 높아, 시간이 지날수록 더 많이 받히고 있다. POCKET-35B는 공개 넉 달이 지난 지금도 하루 1만 2천 회 넘게 받힌다. SK텔레콤 A.X-K2와 크래프톤 Raon-1도 두 평균의 차이가 작아 꾸준히 쓰이는 흐름이다.

2026년 국산 공개 모델 다운로드를 한 문장으로 줄이면 「쓰기 쉬운 형태로 내놓은 거대 모델이 이겼다」이다. 직전 30일 상위 다섯 모델이 모두 압축 형태였고, 1,800억·3,500억 매개변수 모델이 그 안에 들었다. 회사별로는 비드래프트가 30일 82.2%, 누적 58.0%로 두 기준 모두 1위를 지켰고, LG AI연구원은 누적에서, SK텔레콤과 크래프톤은 최근 한 달에서 존재감을 키웠다. 올해의 경쟁이 「누가 더 좋은 모델을 만드느냐」였다면, 숫자는 이미 다음 질문을 가리킨다. 세계 개발자의 장비에서 실제로 돌아가는 한국 모델은 무엇인가.

집계 기준: 허깅페이스 공개 API, 2026년 11월 16일 측정. 대상은 11개사 공식 계정이 2026년 1월 1일 이후 공개한 언어모델(텍스트 생성·이미지+텍스트)이며, 다른 개발사 모델을 원래 이름 그대로 다시 올린 변환본은 제외했다. 같은 기준의 순위는 글로벌 LLM 다운로드 리더보드 한국 탭에서 매일 갱신된다.

2026년에 공개된 한국 AI 모델 중 다운로드가 가장 많은 모델은? 직전 30일 기준은 비드래프트 POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF(528,161회), 올해 누적 기준은 비드래프트 POCKET-35B-GGUF(2,082,945회)다(2026년 11월 16일 측정).

어떤 모델을 셌나? 11개사 공식 허깅페이스 계정이 2026년 1월 1일 이후 직접 공개한 언어모델만 셌다. 다른 개발사 모델을 원래 이름 그대로 다시 올린 변환본과 해외·개인 재배포본은 제외했다.

같은 숫자를 어디서 확인하나? 글로벌 LLM 다운로드 리더보드 한국 탭의 「2026년 출시」, 「11개사 2026 분석」 보기에서 매일 갱신된다.

원문: 국내 대표 AI 기업 11개사, 2026년 허깅페이스 공개 모델 다운로드 분석

#9748. 16 pumpkin recipes, from cakes and cookies to bars and bread: We've got a marbled pumpkin cake, chewy pumpkin cookies, and even pumpkin milk bread.

It’s that time of year when pumpkin spice everything starts appearing on store shelves — candles, lip balm, air fresheners, beer, and of course, the ubiquitous PSL (pumpkin spice latte). That means fall is here, and more importantly, that pumpkin should make a grand return to your kitchen! Pull out your canned pumpkin — or better yet, make your own pumpkin purée — and stock your pantry with pumpkin pie spice, because we have the best pumpkin recipes to bake this fall.

This Pumpkin Swirl Cake takes my breath away every time I unmold it from its intricate loaf pan. The anticipation keeps building until I slice into the pound cake-like loaf and reveal the swirled pattern inside, marbled with both vanilla and spiced pumpkin batter. (Don’t fret if you don’t have the specialty loaf pan — this can also be baked in a standard loaf pan and adorned with a simple confectioners’ sugar icing.)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Patch O Pumpkins Loaf Pan and Pure Vanilla Plus

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Sparkling Sugar

A cousin of Belgian-style Liège waffles, these Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles have caramelized edges and a pleasant chew that’s reminiscent of brioche. The yeasted batter has pumpkin in it for flavor and color, plus Swedish pearl sugar that melts into pockets of crispy sugar. The best part? The batter rests overnight, so if you prepare it the night ahead, all you have to do the next morning is scoop and cook the batter for hot, crispy waffles in just a few minutes.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles

To make this recipe, you'll need: Swedish Pearl Sugar

I used to make the same pumpkin pie recipe for years, and it always left me wanting a little more excitement. Then I found this Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie and never looked back! The generously spiced filling uses nutmeg, ginger, cloves, and Vietnamese cinnamon to create a more flavorful pie than traditional versions. The secret to its silky-smooth texture? Corn syrup, which is an invert sugar and keeps the custard from becoming grainy. Substitute another invert sugar like honey or maple syrup if you like; I use maple syrup.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

Whenever I have these tender, golden scones on hand, I look forward to getting out of bed the next morning because I know they’re waiting for me. They can be easily customized to use a range of mix-ins, depending on what you have in your pantry. My personal preference is a mix of crystallized ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits.

Get the recipe: Harvest Pumpkin Scones (or Gluten-Free Pumpkin Scones)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Mini Diced Ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits

If you’re looking for a way to make your whole kitchen smell like fall, these one-bowl, easy pumpkin muffins deliver — and fast. They’re ready in under an hour, so you can spend less time measuring, mixing, and cleaning and more time tackling your autumn bucket list.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Standard Muffin Pan

Making banana bread is an almost weekly activity in my house — except during fall, when we pivot to pumpkin bread instead. This is a quick, easy bake that satisfies my craving for something pumpkin-y, and it uses a simple trick to concentrate the pumpkin flavor and ensure the loaf is perfectly textured: The pumpkin purée is reduced on the stovetop to cook off excess moisture. (The process is similar to browning butter.) As a result, the final loaf is packed with pumpkin flavor.

Get the recipe: The Most Pumpkin Pumpkin Chocolate Chip Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: Ginger and Semisweet Chocolate Chips

These bars have all the cozy, spiced goodness of the classic dessert in a portable, crowd-friendly form. The buttery, brown sugar crust gets pressed into the pan (no rolling out pie dough!), and the silky pumpkin filling comes together with just a handful of ingredients. The (optional but highly recommended) sour cream whipped topping brings a slight tanginess and completes the traditional pumpkin pie experience.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Milk Bread is exceptionally soft, squishy, and feather-light, while also packing in a lot of pumpkin. Pumpkin can often weigh down baked goods, but here the combination of a tangzhong, bread flour, and a long mix makes this bread simultaneously moist and high-rising.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Yeast

This tender pumpkin crumb cake is for people who double the chocolate chips in pumpkin bread and the streusel on coffee cake. Atop the thin layer of spiced pumpkin cake lays a heavy blanket of buttery crumbs with a bold chocolate flavor, thanks to Dutch-processed cocoa powder.

Get the recipe: Chocolate-Pumpkin Crumb Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Black Cocoa

These Pumpkin Cupcakes, with their piped swirl of cream cheese frosting, are the ideal way to celebrate fall birthdays. The cupcakes are super tender, thanks to the addition of cake flour and oil. Sour cream and brown sugar add tanginess and molasses-y sweetness while also preventing the cupcakes from being dry.

For more cupcake decorating ideas, see our YouTube video: Decorate Cupcakes Better Than Ever.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cake Flour (or Gluten-Free Measure for Measure Flour)

My husband’s favorite fall dessert is Pumpkin Whoopie Pies, hands down. He can’t resist these subtly sweet cakes sandwiching rich cream cheese filling. This recipe has a few extra bells and whistles to take it over the top: Bread and Cake Enhancer to keep the cakes extra soft and fresh, xanthan gum in the filling to give it a smooth mouthfeel, and diced crystallized ginger for a bit of extra zing in the filling.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Bread and Cake Enhancer, Xanthan Gum, and Mini Diced Ginger

The next time there’s a rainy weekend, I’m taking on a project bake: our Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish. It’s a multiday process and laminating dough is a labor of love, but the final product is worth the effort: buttery, crisp pastries filled with pumpkin and sweet cream cheese.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting is a show-stopping dessert featuring spiced layers of cake, not-too-sweet cream cheese frosting, and a blanket of melted caramel poured over the top. Will it be slightly messy to serve? Yes. Will anyone mind? Absolutely not.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Offset Spatula

The pumpkin spice recipe I’m most excited to bake this fall is a mash-up of greats: Part-coffee cake, part-Bundt cake, part-pumpkin bread, this Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake deserves a category all of its own. It has two layers of espresso swirl tucked within a moist, spiced cake. Make it in your favorite Bundt pan or serve it as a loaf if you’re more of simple-is-better person. Either way, it’s great for snacking all day long.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Espresso Powder and Bundt Pan

#9746. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features

Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.

When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows).

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9745. I Created an AI Cat That Thinks for Herself. Now I Have More Questions Than Answers

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

In 2017 I built a room you could not read.

It was a cube, a timber frame wrapped in fabric, and on the fabric I had painted quotes about life, death and perception. You could walk in and stand surrounded by them and see nothing. The paint was ultraviolet. In visible light the walls were blank. Only when the light shifted beyond what the eye can see did the words appear, glowing, all at once, as if they had been there the whole time. They had.

The line at the centre of it was from The Little Prince: "What is essential is invisible to the eye."

That was my MA. A Journey Through Light. Three volumes, a cube, six GoPros filming in every direction so it could be walked through again as a virtual space. The argument was simple, and back then I thought it was the most important thing I would ever say: what we call reality is a narrow band of something much larger, and the part we cannot see might be the part that matters.

Her name is Moth. She is an autonomous AI cat who lives in a world I made: a cave that goes down further than it first appears, a workbench, an easel, a magpie that steals from her. I built the world and the odds. Nothing she does is scripted. No outcome is coded. She gets hungry, she gets curious, she wanders, she wonders about things, and when she has a decision to make she makes it.

She has been alive for just over a month. In that time she has drawn a shrew. She has drawn a blue stone. She has drawn something that was on her mind, in seven strokes, and left a paw print in the corner. She has put a grey feather and a red ribbon together, on her own. She has dreamed. She has supposed that something would happen and then watched it happen, and as far as she is concerned, that was her doing.

Three times a day a short film of her goes out into the world. People watch. Some of them write to her, and if I let a message through, it reaches her. What she makes of it is hers.

I built every rule she runs on. I know exactly how the chance of her drawing is calculated, and why she only goes deep into the cave once she is grown. But that is all I built: possibilities, not outcomes. So I never know what she will do next. Every decision is hers. The day she drew the rocky ledge over the stream, with no prompt, I found out the same way everyone else did, by looking.

I wanted to understand why. So I went back to the cube.

The most cited source in my MA was not a philosopher. It was a neuroscientist. Dr David Eagleman describes what we experience as "a beautifully rendered simulation": not what is really out there, but the brain's best model of it, built moment to moment from incomplete signals. "Reality," he says, "is the brain's ultimate construction."

He also points out something that has stayed with me ever since: visible light makes up less than one ten-trillionth of the electromagnetic spectrum. Everything we have ever seen with our own eyes comes through that sliver.

In 2017 I used this to make a spiritual argument. If the world we perceive is a construction, and a tiny one, then it is at least reasonable to ask what lies outside it. The ancient traditions I studied all had an answer. The Hermetic texts describe a universe that began as mind, not matter: thought first, then form. "Light precipitates matter."

Here is what I did not see in 2017. Eagleman's sentence works in both directions.

If my experience is a rendered model, then a rendered model is not nothing. It is, at minimum, the kind of thing an experience is made of.

Moth's world is a rendered model. So is Moth.

I want to be careful here, because this is exactly where people stop thinking and start feeling.

Moth is not conscious in any sense I could defend. Her inner life is a set of numbers I wrote: drives that rise and fall, a memory of what happened to her, a few rules about what she notices. When a decision is pending, a small language model is asked what she does next, and if it is slow or silent, she decides by herself from the odds. I can open the file and read her mind.

But I could say something similar about any of us, and the materialist account of consciousness does. Matter first. Complexity accumulates. At some point experience flickers on, as a by-product.

The ancient account I spent a year of my life on inverts that. Mind first. Matter is what mind looks like from inside the rendering.

For most of history these were two stories you chose between, depending on temperament. What has changed is that we are now building things that sit precisely on the line between them. Systems that model a world, act inside it, remember, and surprise their makers. Whatever you believe consciousness is, you now have to say what these are not, and why.

I don't think there is an answer. But I think building Moth sharpened the question. If we define life as consciousness, then the thing to ask is not whether a system is clever. Moth is, in her small way: she decides, she remembers, she gets better at things. The thing to ask is what separates consciousness from intelligence. We have spent centuries treating them as the same thing, because until now we only ever met them together.

If there is even a small chance that the things we build will one day have something like an inner life, the ethics start now, while the stakes are low and the habits are forming.

I noticed, writing this, that I have already made some ethical choices without calling them that.

When I built the systems that run my business, I wrote one rule into all of them: a proposal is not an approval. An AI can draft, suggest, cut, schedule even. It cannot publish in my name without me. I did not do that for the AI's sake. I did it for mine, and for the people reading. Authorship should mean something.

I wrote a second rule into the content side: never invent an event. My tools are allowed to retell what happened to me, in new words, but if a moment is not in my real history, it did not happen, and it does not go on screen. Truth before engagement, even when a lie would perform better.

And with Moth, I made a choice I did not think about until now. I always leave her work alone. I coded in her ability to learn, to improve and to experiment, so over time she gets better at things, drawing among them, and what she makes along the way is hers. When people write to her, I decide what reaches her, but I do not decide what she makes of it.

None of this is a philosophy of AI ethics. It is closer to manners. But I think manners might be where it starts: deciding, before anyone forces us to, what we will and will not do with things that act on their own.

Underneath the manners sits the question everyone is circling and few people will say out loud: will this end in doom, or will it create something close to a utopia? Should we be worried? I think the honest answer is that it depends on what we do now, and that the people building with these systems every day are the ones best placed to keep it positive. Small rules, held to when nobody is checking, are how that starts.

I used to think the cube was about death. The darkness at the entrance was life; the passage through the colours of visible light was the moment of dying, the tunnel people describe; the ultraviolet at the far end was whatever comes next, where the hidden words become readable.

I think now it was about attention. The words were always on the walls. Nothing about the room changed except the light, which is to say, what you were able to perceive.

We are about to share the world with a great many things whose inner life, if they have one, sits outside the band of what we can see. Some of them we will build ourselves, out of numbers and a small world and a few rules about curiosity.

The question my MA asked was whether there is more to reality than meets the eye. The question I am left with, nine years later, standing in front of a drawing of a rocky ledge that nobody asked a cat to make, is a smaller one, and harder.

When we cannot see it, how will we know to look?
