#9740. ACHNET's Talent Personality Questionnaire (TPQ) Starts With the Job Description, Then the Candidate

ACHNET's Talent Personality Questionnaire (TPQ) Starts With the Job Description, Then Asks About the Candidate

The Talent Personality Questionnaire reads a candidate's working preferences against competencies chosen for each role, and tells the hiring manager what to ask in the interview.

Two candidates can describe their working style in exactly the same way and still be different hires. A preference for adapting as situations change may carry particular importance in one role, while planning, consistency and execution may receive greater weight in another. The appropriate balance depends on the responsibilities of the position. A personality profile read on its own cannot tell a hiring manager which of those situations applies.

That gap is what ACHNET set out to close with its Talent Personality Questionnaire, or TPQ, which is available as part of its Unified Talent Selection Platform. TPQ begins with the vacancy. The hiring team supplies a job description or the role's key responsibility areas, and the questionnaire and its report are configured around what that position demands before a candidate answers a single question.

Configuration runs through iJupiter™, the AI Super Agent at the center of ACHNET's platform. From the job description or responsibility areas, iJupiter™ recommends which competencies matter for the role, how they should be prioritized, what level each should reach, and how much weight each carries in the final profile. The hiring team reviews those recommendations and adjusts them before the questionnaire goes out.

Most of TPQ's design follows from that sequence. In ACHNET's view, a general personality profile leaves the hiring manager to work out what it means for the vacancy in front of them.

"A general personality description may provide context, but hiring teams still need to understand what that information means for the position they are filling," said Manouj Gupta, CEO of ACHNET.

The questionnaire uses a forced-choice format. Candidates see groups of three statements and pick the one most like them and the one least like them. Each statement in a set can sound reasonable, so a candidate cannot rate all three highly and has to show which preferences come first.

Forced-choice formats are used in personality assessment partly to address applicants' tendency to present themselves favorably. A 2019 meta-analysis in the Journal of Applied Psychology by Mengyang Cao and Fritz Drasgow reported an overall standardized score-inflation effect size of 0.06 across the forced-choice measures studied. In selection settings, inflation was lower than comparison estimates for single-statement measures across most personality facets, although findings varied with questionnaire design and scoring.

The same study carries a caution that applies directly to a role-configured tool. Cao and Drasgow found that the facets most relevant to the target job showed more inflation than facets with little bearing on it. The inflation is largest, in other words, on the traits an employer is most likely to be looking for. A questionnaire built around one role's competencies asks about exactly those traits, so a format that limits inflation matters more for TPQ than it would for a general personality inventory.

TPQ measures 35 competencies grouped into six domains. They are Cognitive and Strategic Capabilities, Interpersonal Effectiveness, Self-Management, Execution, Integrity, and Adaptability. Between them, they cover how a person approaches thinking, collaboration, managing their own work, delivery, responsible behavior, and change.

Different roles can assign different priorities, target levels, and weights to the competencies being evaluated. TPQ uses an adaptive approach in which questions can adjust based on previous responses to explore relevant behavioral areas further. The resulting profile is interpreted against the configured requirements of the role.

The output is a role-configured competency profile. It sets out where a candidate's stated preferences match what the role needs, where there may be gaps, and which areas a hiring manager should explore further in conversation with the candidate.

The report can help hiring managers identify areas for follow-up. In a 2022 re-analysis, Paul Sackett, Charlene Zhang, Christopher Berry and Filip Lievens revised earlier estimates of how well selection methods predict job performance, with structured interviews emerging as the highest-ranked procedure examined. That finding does not validate TPQ's interview prompts. Structured interviews require standardized questions and consistent scoring criteria; TPQ's prompts provide additional areas to explore.

ACHNET is explicit about how far the questionnaire's findings should be taken.

"TPQ supports human judgment. It should not be presented as a pass/fail test, a fixed personality label, or a definitive predictor of job performance," Gupta said.

The company presents the report as material for a conversation. The same findings can carry past the hiring decision, into onboarding priorities and development discussions once the candidate has joined.

TPQ is one stage in ACHNET's platform, alongside applicant ranking, technical assessments, AI video interviews conducted by iJupiter™ and fraud detection. Each produces a different kind of evidence. A resume records experience and qualifications. A technical assessment provides evidence of a candidate's knowledge or skills in the areas assessed. TPQ adds a structured account of how the candidate prefers to work, interpreted against the demands of the specific role.

Holding those inputs in one place lets a hiring team weigh them together when it reaches a decision. Reviewing these inputs together gives hiring teams a broader view of the candidate's experience, demonstrated skills, and workplace behavioral preferences. TPQ contributes one source of evidence alongside assessments, interviews, and other role-relevant information.

TPQ asks about the competencies a specific job needs, makes candidates choose between their own preferences, and passes what it finds to the person running the interview. How much it improves a hire will depend on what that person does with the report, and ACHNET has left that decision with the hiring team.

#9739. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

#9737. 9 Ranch Dressing Brands With High-Quality Ingredients

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Ranch is one of the most popular salad dressings and dips in the country. But many of the tangy products are made with less-than-ideal ingredients. That's why we've created this list of organic and clean-ingredient ranch brands. Not only do dressings with high-quality ingredients generally taste better due to the lack of fillers, but they're healthier, too. That's thanks to the products being made without artificial ingredients or synthetic preservatives. The fact that you can use less and still get a lot of flavor makes these an economical choice, as well.

Because these brands use minimal stabilizers and preservatives, it's important to know they won't last as long as other shelf-stable ranch dressings. Usually, a bottle of ranch can stay safe for up to three months after opening, but with these companies' products often using real dairy, it's best to treat them more like homemade. That means it's safest to consume these dressings within one month of opening, although some can last up to two months. But with all the different ways you can use ranch, leftovers shouldn't be a problem.

Primal Kitchen was founded in 2015 as a way to bring clean-ingredient condiments to the public. Today, it sells over 80 products, such as organic unsweetened ketchup, steak sauce, and mayonnaise made with avocado oil. The company uses plant-based oils and other high-quality ingredients in its ranch, which has no added sugars or conventional stabilizers. Primal Kitchen Ranch, which can be found in many grocery stores, is also made with cage-free eggs, is certified Keto-safe and gluten-free, and is Whole30 approved.

This product is dairy-free, relying on a mix of organic apple cider vinegar, spices, herbs, and egg yolks to create the rich, tangy taste of ranch. Mushroom extract takes the place of synthetic preservatives to keep the dressing fresh, and the dip's base is made from avocado oil-based mayo. In fact, many of Primal Kitchen's dressings and sauces contain avocado oil because it's a sustainable source of monounsaturated fats that are linked to lowering "bad" LDL cholesterol and reducing blood pressure.

Reviewers have reported the sauce having a distinctly herby taste, with pronounced dill that wasn't overwhelming. The dressing is great as is, but feel free to add a bit of lime to turn the ranch into the base for incredible nachos. Or if you want an unexpectedly delicious flavor, add some edible lavender to the dip. The aromatic flower complements the heavier sauce and makes this a wonderful addition to a chopped veggies board.

Ohio-based slaw and salad dressing company Marzetti was founded way back in 1896. Today, it's respected enough by customers to have ranked No. 32 in the Food and Beverage section on Newsweek's list of the Most Trustworthy Companies in America in 2026. So it's probably not surprising to learn that Marzetti has earned not just one, but two spots on this list.

This first one is for the Classic Ranch Dressing. This product is made without artificial flavors, preservatives, or high fructose corn syrup. It also uses actual buttermilk instead of powder, giving it an authentic tangy taste and a creamy consistency. The brand sells it in a refrigerated 13-ounce option or as a 22-ounce shelf-stable bottle. Fans of the classic ranch have praised the product's taste and versatility, alongside the fact that the larger version comes in a squeeze bottle, allowing them to easily portion out exactly how much they'd like.

Created by a woman who wanted to ensure the dressing she was using was healthy, Tessemae's makes its products without artificial ingredients, and every ranch in its line of six is Whole30-approved and made without any elements harvested from genetically modified organisms (GMOs). The company's Organic Creamy Ranch Dressing & Dip doesn't have any fillers either; plus it's gluten- and dairy-free, as well as certified USDA organic.

The sauce uses cage-free eggs in the base, alongside organic high oleic sunflower oil, lemon juice, and mustard. This results in a thick, luscious mix that's flavored by various spices and herbs, with tanginess from distilled vinegar. The plant-based dressing is suitable for those following a keto or vegetarian lifestyle. And even though this version is different from the original 1950s ranch recipe, it's still great for marinating fried chicken, serving as a dip for pizza, or simply pouring on salad greens.

Walden Farms is so dedicated to customer satisfaction that the company changed the way it makes its dressings. After hearing people ask for cleaner ingredients, it reformulated the recipes it uses for products like the Ranch Dressing. The dip is now made with olive oil and no artificial flavors. It's also gluten-free and low-calorie, so it can appeal to a wider audience.

The ranch is low-carb, too, with only 1 gram per serving. Being plant-based, it's suitable for vegetarian lifestyles, and it's still made with no sugars, so it's friendly for diabetic people, as well. There are 30 calories per serving, and the olive oil base ensures this dressing only has three grams of total fat in each portion. If you're interested in trying Walden Farms ranch, you can use it in your next batch of mac and cheese along with corn kernels for some nice pops of sweetness.

Drew's Organics doesn't use GMO ingredients or any artificial flavors or colors in any of its dressings. That includes the Creamy Ranch Dressing & Quick Marinade, which is made without artificial preservatives, added sugars, high-fructose corn syrup, or trans fats. The ranch dressing also works as a great marinade for a juicy pork roast or chicken, thanks to its combination of fat, sodium, and vinegars. In fact, reviewers have noted the ranch has a wonderfully oniony taste, with a thick enough texture to stick to a salad or side of fries.

It's also made with organic high oleic sunflower oil, which is a heart-healthy alternative to heavier fats, thanks to being high in monounsaturated fatty acids. These MUFAs are associated with lowering insulin resistance, inflammation, and cardiovascular diseases, according to research published in the Annals of Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism. If this is your first time encountering it, high-oleic oil acts like extra virgin olive oil when cooking because the two have very similar fat amounts and types.

Toby's Family Foods has been around since 1978. The company specializes in making each of its eight dressings in batches small enough that every one of them can still be made by hand. There are regular sauces, as well as probiotic ones, including a ranch made with yogurt as a base. Toby's regular Ranch Dressing & Dip is made with clean ingredients, such as buttermilk from cows that aren't given rBST, a synthetic growth hormone that's been linked to certain forms of cancer.

The ranch doesn't use artificial flavors, preservatives, MSG, or synthetic stabilizers, so it has a shorter refrigeration window after opening. Instead of one to two months, Toby's recommends the sauce be finished within two weeks. It also uses non-GMO canola oil that's obtained through high-pressure processing to keep as many of the vitamins and flavor intact as possible. That oil can sometimes separate from the dairy in the ranch, but all you have to do to recombine it is shake or stir the bottle's contents a bit.

Briannas has a long line of dressings and sauces made with high-quality ingredients. The brand's Traditional Ranch is a newer product that, while similar to its Classic Buttermilk Ranch, has fewer calories per serving. This option is also gluten-free, vegetarian, and Kosher Certified.

It's made without high-fructose corn syrup, which many companies use as a cheaper alternative to natural sugars. However, large amounts of high-fructose corn syrup have been linked to liver inflammation, making it something you might want to steer clear of in general. Made in Brenham, Texas, Briannas ranch doesn't have trans fats and is manufactured in a facility without the potential for cross-contamination from nuts.

#9734. Not Regular Butter Or Mayo: Use This Spread To Give Breakfast Burritos A Delicious, Crunchy Exterior

Breakfast burritos originated in Santa Fe, New Mexico, and have now become a popular way to start the day across the U.S. — they are even available at McDonald's! The typical combination of eggs, meats, and cheese wrapped in a tortilla is not only packed with flavor and protein but is also a conveniently portable food.

There are many variations on a breakfast burrito recipe, such as changing up the type of cheese or switching up the meats, but these ignore what holds it all together: the tortilla. You can just wrap your fillings in one and call it a day, but you know that it's much better (and crunchier) when you toast it, and you need a little fat to get the job done. Butter is a great solution, but using garlic butter will impart so much additional flavor to your finished breakfast burrito.

Garlic butter isn't some type of fat made from garlic, though. Instead, it's part of a larger category of foods called compound butters, which consist of regular dairy butter blended with a variety of seasonings and other ingredients to add flavor. Since many herbs and spices contain fat-soluble flavor compounds, the butter becomes infused with the aromas of whatever is added to it, including garlic. So, when you toast your breakfast burrito in garlic butter, the fat itself has a garlicky kick that will get transferred to your tortilla. It will also save you the hassle of frying garlic in butter to get a similar effect.

To make your breakfast burrito extra crispy with garlic butter, you simply need to wrap your burrito in a flour tortilla, which is the most flexible for making this breakfast favorite and tends to come in larger sizes compared to corn tortillas. You can assemble several burritos this way if you want to meal prep. Then, melt about a tablespoon of garlic butter in a pan over medium heat and place your burrito in the pan seam-side down to seal it. Turn it over to toast the other side, and promptly remove it from the pan. For more even browning, you can place a flat tortilla in the pan, add all your fillings, and then remove it to roll up, making sure to tuck in the sides. You can also grease a muffin tin with garlic butter to make breakfast burrito bites.

There are many commercially available garlic butters you can find at supermarkets, including one made by Kerrygold, but they can often be more expensive per ounce than regular butter, even from premium brands. Fortunately, compound butters — including variations on plain garlic butter — are very easy to make at home. David Guas' roasted garlic compound butter, for example, can be frozen for up to three months and is customizable. You can add finely minced herbs, like parsley and thyme. If you don't have fresh herbs, you can also use dried versions, though give your compound butter some extra time for the flavors to marry.

#9730. 11 Common Mistakes Everyone Makes When Peeling Fruit

There's lots of chatter online about the best ways to peel all kinds of fruit, and the debate may just rage on forever. Regardless of how you feel about the many creative methods that seem to gain so much attention, there are a few mistakes you would be wise to avoid. Why? Well, when you sidestep these common blunders, you not only cut down on unnecessary waste, but also create less of a mess along the way and speed up the process as a whole. Sounds like a win-win-win to us.

From peeling your bananas in the wrong direction to trying to peel tomatoes without blanching them first to not utilizing a spoon to help you scoop avocado meat from the skin, many of the missteps found below are ones plenty of people commit every day. So, even if you think you already know the best way to peel a particular type of fruit, you may be surprised to learn there's a more efficient or tidy way to get the job done. Are you already in the know, or are you falling prey to frequent mistakes unbeknownst to you? Let's find out.

You'd be hard-pressed to find someone who hasn't tried to peel an orange using nothing but their hands before. However, doing so is the first fruit-peeling mistake on our list. If you've ever done it that way and found yourself attempting to remove the white, stringy pith to no avail, you already know why, too. Thankfully, though, there's a way to avoid this and cut down on the bothersome, bitter-tasting membranes, and it isn't complicated. All you need to do is employ a little help from a knife. Not only will it get the job done quickly and correctly, but it'll also save you from having to scrape remnants of the orange peel from under your fingernails as well — and most of us are all too familiar with how annoying that can be.

To peel an orange while avoiding the majority of the pith (aka the right way), start by setting it on a cutting board stem side up. Then, use an extra-sharp knife to make a vertical cut just off the side of the stem, straight down to the bottom. Continue doing this four times in total, in a box shape, so you are left with a rectangular center piece. The middle section will contain most of the pith, so feel free to toss it out. After that, you can simply enjoy the four orange wedges straight from the peel. It's that easy.

A major complaint people have about peaches is that they don't enjoy consuming the fuzzy skin very much. As a result, knowing how to peel them will serve you well. Even so, many people don't even think about removing the skin, or they reach for a peeling tool, and unfortunately, that's a mistake with the gentle fruit. While handy, the kitchen tool is much too abrasive for the tender skin and meat of a peach, so they rip right through them and often leave you with a juicy mess and significantly less fruit to enjoy. Nobody wants that. Luckily, there's a better way. You just need to blanch and shock the peaches quickly, and the skins will basically slide right off.

To utilize the blanch and shock method, start by cutting a small X pattern into the bottom of whole peaches. Then, lower them into a pot of boiling water with a slotted spoon. Leave the peaches in the boiling water for about 1 to 3 minutes, depending on how ripe they are — the riper they are, the less time they'll need, but you'll know they are done when the scored sections start to peel back. After that, remove the peaches and submerge them in an ice bath to quickly cool them off and prevent them from cooking. After about five minutes, extract the peaches and use your hands to quickly and easily peel back the skins, starting from the scored section.

Mangoes are a stone (or drupe) fruit. As such, they contain a large pit in the center, and this can make peeling them complicated, especially since the flesh is so tender. However, you can easily manage the task if you utilize the best method for peeling mangoes, which involves scoring a grid pattern in the outer portions of the mango after the core is removed. When you do, you are left with simple-to-remove cubes of fruit that are perfect for munching solo or incorporating into recipes of all kinds.

To start, set a mango on a cutting board and hold it upright with the stem at the top. The next step is to use a sharp knife to make vertical cuts from the top to bottom on all four sides about ¼ inch from the center. This removes the pit and leaves you with four sides containing all the good stuff. After that, use your knife to score a grid pattern in each portion, taking care not to cut through the skin itself. When this is done, push up from the skin side so you wind up with rows of protruding cubes of fruit. All that's left for you to do at this point is to use a spoon to scoop them out. Your knife will work as a scoop as well, but the room for error increases, as it can easily cut through the skin. So, if you want to play it safe, spoon it is.

Peeling tomatoes seems like a challenging task, but it must be done if you want to turn them into a basic sauce or can them. The skins are relatively tough, and the fruit beneath is tender enough to fall apart with minimal pressure from a knife or peeling tool. Don't even get us started on how easily the juice squeezes out, either. In fact, the process is daunting enough that many people simply reach for canned tomatoes to avoid the mess and effort, which can feel futile if you don't do it the right way. Speaking of which, the best, easiest way to peel tomatoes starts with blanching them, so don't make the mistake of attempting to get the job done without doing so.

Blanching tomatoes may sound fancy to some, but it couldn't be simpler. To start. Bring a pot of water to a rolling boil. While you wait, score small X patterns into the bottom of the tomatoes you wish to peel. When the water is ready, drop them in and leave them for about 30 to 40 seconds; anything longer than that and you run the risk of the fruit becoming too mushy to handle. Then, extract them from the water with a slotted spoon and put them directly into an ice bath. After about two to three minutes, you can start pulling them out and using your hands to quickly and easily slide the tomato skins off.

You don't have to peel apples to enjoy them — the skins are edible, after all. Still, if you want to hone in on the tart, sweet fruit below without the peels getting in the way, or add them to a recipe that calls for skinned ones, removing them is always an option. However, there are many methods people employ, some of which are much more effective than others. With this in mind, choosing not to utilize what has been deemed the donut ring method is a mistake. It is quick, easy, and helps minimize waste as well. Since that's the goal, you're going to want to commit it to memory.

Whether you prefer to use a paring knife or a vegetable peeler, the donut ring method is the way to go when it comes to peeling apples. Regardless of your preferred tool, start by cutting a ring around the top and bottom of your apple. Then, use your knife or peeler to slice vertically from top to bottom, connecting the two initial circles.

Once you are all done, you don't have to toss the stem and skin into the trash, either. Instead, you can completely eliminate waste by making a Peel-To-Stem Apple Pie. We know this sounds counterintuitive since we spend so much time removing them in the first place, but don't knock it until you try it.

Pear skins are edible, but there are plenty of times when peeling them is in order, such as when you are making a pie or canning them. The skins aren't very tough, either, so using a vegetable peeler isn't off the table. However, if you need to peel more than one, there's a much easier way to achieve your goal: Blanching and shocking them. This isn't the first time we've said this about peeling fruit, but with pears, it truly is a game-changer that allows the skins to simply slide right off with the brush of your fingers. So, choosing not to use the method when peeling batches of pears would be a time-consuming blunder you don't want to commit.

To properly blanch pears, submerge them in a pot of water that is boiling or just under. As long as the water is piping hot, it'll work its skin-peeling magic. Leave the fruit in the pot for about 10 seconds, maybe 15 at most. Then, remove one and drop it into a bowl of ice-cold water. Before removing the rest of the pears from the pot, check them to make sure you left the extracted one in the hot water long enough by rubbing the skin. If it comes off easily, transfer the remaining pears to the ice bath. If not, pop the initial pear back in the hot water for a few more seconds before removing them all.

Pineapple is arguably the best tropical fruit of them all, but even if you don't feel that way, it is a tricky fruit to peel. The outer layer of eyes is extremely dense and hard, so it's not like a vegetable peeler will do the trick. A sharp knife is undoubtedly a must. However, where you begin the cutting process matters, and not starting by creating a flat base is not the way to go. If you skip ahead of the step, the pineapple's curved bottom makes slicing precarious and unstable at best.

Thankfully, creating a stable base on a pineapple is easy-peasy, and then the rest of the peeling process effortlessly falls into place. Simply lay the fruit on its side and grip the top while slicing through the base to create a flat end piece. Then, do the same on the top and stand the entire fruit upright. From there, cut the hard core out by slicing from the top to bottom on all four sides, leaving a small rectangular cube in the center. After that, you can slice the fleshy parts of the pineapple into cubes, long slices, or however you like.

Papayas have a distinct musky flavor backed up by lots of sweetness. While some say it is an acquired taste, there's almost nothing that compares once you develop it. Even so, it contains lots of small black seeds, which, while edible, bring a strong, mustardy, peppery, bitter element to the table that most people don't want to munch along with the fruit itself. With this in mind, knowing how to peel a papaya properly is essential. The first mistake people often commit is trying to skin a papaya whole. It may be easy to do, but once the fruit is peeled, it becomes slippery, making it challenging to handle and remove the seeds. That's why it is important to cut the ends off and halve it first.

After halving a whole papaya, the seeds inside are fully exposed, allowing you to easily scoop them out with nothing more than a spoon. Whether you save them to add to another dish or not is up to you, but if it's the sweet, fleshy fruit you are after, the job is nearly done at this point. All that's left is to slide a paring knife just above the skin to separate it from the fruit. Then, you can slice or chop it however you like.

Pomegranates are nutrient-dense and rich in antioxidants, making them a healthy fruit to enjoy. They also boast a deliciously unique sweet, tangy, tart flavor profile that many love. Unfortunately, though, getting to the tasty edible seeds within the fruit isn't as simple as you might hope. Pomegranates contain loads of pith, the seeds don't separate super easily, and the potent red fruit stains like no other, so if you happen to break open a few seeds along the way, your hands or clothes could show the signs of it for quite some time. Thankfully, there is a quick fix for all of these issues: Peeling them underwater. When you do, the colorful juice dilutes before it gets a chance to stain, the pith floats to the top, and the seeds come apart significantly easier. The underwater method also reduces waste, making it the absolute best way to go.

There isn't any fancy trick to using the underwater method for peeling pomegranates. Simply crack open the fruit and submerge it in a bowl of water. Using your hands, start to break apart the seeds and watch as the pith and outer peel float to the top. When all of the seeds are separated, use a slotted spoon to remove the floating waste. Finish off by extracting the seeds and placing them on a paper towel or clean cloth to dry.

Avocados feature a whole slew of health benefits, such as being high in fiber, nutrients, and healthy fats. They are even widely considered a superfood, so knowing how to tap into their potential, i.e., being able to peel them like a pro, is something everyone should know how to do. Regardless, the tough outer shell and large, hard seed in the middle of the avocado mean there are some good and bad ways to peel them. Not using a spoon to help you manage the task is one such mistake you don't want to commit because, plain and simple, it makes the job more complicated than it needs to be.

The best way to peel an avocado starts by slicing into the fruit lengthwise around the seed until you create a complete ring. Then, holding one hand on either side, gently twist, and the two halves should come apart easily, at least if it is ripe. Next, smack your knife into the seed with enough force that it sticks. Twist the knife, and the seed should come right out. Now the two halves are ready for you to slice or cube as desired. Choose your shape and use your knife to create either strips or a grid pattern, taking care not to puncture the skin below. Then, you can easily use a spoon to scoop out the avocado chunks and enjoy.

Interestingly, the way people peel a banana is somewhat of a controversial topic. Do you start at the stem at the top or the nub at the bottom? Many people simply grab a banana and start peeling from the stem without even thinking about it. However, plenty of others claim that is the wrong way, and instead, reach for the bottom nub and hold the stem like a handle — just like monkeys do. While the debate may never end on Reddit and other online forums, we are fans of the "monkey method."

When you use the stem as a handle, you can grip a banana much more firmly without worrying about potentially bruising the delicate fruit inside the peel — something that happens more easily than you might think. In addition, all it takes to split open the skin near the bottom nub is a gentle pinch. Then, you can simply peel back small strips and start munching or dicing as you please. When you go about it the opposite way — what many think is backwards — it takes more force to split the stem from the skin, and it's much easier to smush some of the fruit inside. No, thanks. Neither way may be 100% wrong, but give the monkey method a try and something tells us you'll never look back again. Besides, who can argue with a cute little built-in handle?

#9727. Skip The Oven: This Easy Turkey Dinner Is Ready In Half The Time

With Thanksgiving just around the corner, many of us are gearing up to spend time with friends and family, and enjoy a delicious meal. For those who are hosting and doing the cooking, however, there is considerably more to the holiday. Aside from cleaning the house top to bottom, preparing a huge meal, including a whole turkey, can be stressful to say the least. Eschewing the turkey might take a major burden off your plate, but if you don't want to go fully historical with your Thanksgiving feast (the Plymouth settlers likely ate different game birds and venison) you might instead opt for oven-free, skillet-cooked turkey meatballs in a savory gravy.

Meatballs are an excellent option because you can stuff the flavors of Thanksgiving turkey and stuffing into them, minus the hours of cook time. In fact, if you consider a 20 pound turkey takes four to five hours to roast, and making turkey meatballs takes an hour, tops (depending on how long it takes you to roll them all out), you're saving yourself a lot of time. It also means your oven is completely free for all the delicious sides, like hopefully mistake-free green bean casserole and hot, pillowy rolls. Further, this is a great meal to pull out any time of the year when you want a Thanksgiving turkey-like dinner, without the fuss.

If you're looking for inspiration on what ingredients to use in your turkey meatballs, we have some suggestions (and it's worth noting that none of these ideas add any significant time to the meatball preparation). It's not the best idea to use straight ground turkey because it tends to be quite lean; as you can see in the video above, the creator also includes Italian sausage, which has much-needed fat to help keep the balls moist and tender. If you don't want to use sausage, though, you could take Ina Garten's advice and use prosciutto, or see if you can find ground turkey thighs, as opposed to breast meat, because it has a higher fat content.

Of course to get that real Thanksgiving dinner taste, you'll also want to use plenty of herbs. Sage has a savory, meaty flavor that will boldly season those meatballs, while thyme adds warmth and earthiness; both are often used in stuffing, and they'll pair nicely with your ground turkey and sausage as well. A little rosemary brings a peppery, piney flavor into the mix, and parsley brightens with its herbaceousness.

For a sweet spin that adds another element of a popular Thanksgiving dish, toss in some dried cranberries that have been diced into little bits as well, or try pomegranate-infused Craisins. A touch of citrus zest, too, incorporates some sweetness and complexity.

#9725. Alexey Gubarev: Why Investors Are Finally Taking Women's Health Seriously

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

The Business Research Company reports that the global femtech market was worth about $46.5 billion in 2025 and could reach nearly $119 billion by 2030, with an annual growth rate of 20.8%. So, how did femtech move from a niche category to a major investment opportunity, and why are investors now taking women's health seriously? Alexey Gubarev, a tech entrepreneur based in Cyprus, offers his view.

He co-founded Palta, the venture company behind Flo Health, which became the first women’s health app valued at over $1 billion in 2024. He also built Servers.com, a global infrastructure company he led for 18 years before it was sold for $200 million in 2023.

For many years, women's health was seen as a small part of healthcare. Topics like menstruation, fertility, and pregnancy were viewed as specialist areas instead of being recognized as the basis for a much larger healthcare market. Because of this, technology investors often provided limited funding, set cautious valuations, and believed that women's health products had limited growth potential.

That perception is finally beginning to change.

It's not just that women's health is now a more visible social issue. Investors are beginning to see how big the unmet need is, how large the potential market could be, and the chance to build lasting global businesses around problems that have been overlooked for generations.

After years of building technology companies and investing in digital health, I see femtech as one of the most exciting opportunities where technology, healthcare, and consumer behavior meet.

The women's health gap is not a new problem. Research by the McKinsey Health Institute, published in collaboration with the World Economic Forum in 2024, found that women spend approximately 25% more of their lives in poor health than men. The report estimated that addressing this gap could add up to $1 trillion to the global economy annually by 2040.

In the past, medical research and healthcare systems often did not fully consider women's specific needs. Because of this, many conditions were under-researched, underdiagnosed, or not properly addressed. Women have frequently faced complex health questions without reliable, personalized information.

When we established Palta in 2016, our ambition was to empower billions of health-conscious people to live healthier and happier lives. Women's health quickly emerged as one of the clearest opportunities to make a meaningful difference. I talked about the early years at Palta and the apps we started with in this interview with CBN.

About half of the world's population experiences menstruation, but for years there was no credible, technology-based product to address this need on a global scale. We noticed a huge gap between the size of the problem and the solutions that existed.

For investors, this gap should have been a clear sign. Instead, the sector was often seen as niche and overlooked.

In recent years, more digital products have been created to meet women's health needs. What started as a small category focused on period-tracking apps has grown into a much wider range of platforms that cover fertility, pregnancy, hormonal conditions, menopause, and access to specialized medical care.

Several companies illustrate how diverse this market has become.

For example, Maven Clinic has created a virtual healthcare platform that covers fertility, family planning, pregnancy, parenting, and menopause. In October 2024, the company raised $125 million in a Series F round, reaching a reported valuation of $1.7 billion and bringing its total funding to over $425 million. The platform partners with employers and health plans, showing that women's health solutions can also become strong business-to-business healthcare models.

Another example is Midi Health, which focuses on perimenopause, menopause, and midlife women's health. In February 2026, it raised $100 million in Series D funding at a valuation of over $1 billion. This is notable because it shows that investment in women's health is growing beyond fertility and reproductive care into areas that have often been overlooked.

At Palta, we think the best businesses in this field bring together three things: technology that can grow, strong medical expertise, and careful financial management.

The success of Flo and other femtech companies is a big milestone, but it's not the end of the industry's story. It shows what can happen when long-ignored healthcare needs are met with the right mix of technology, science, and good business practices.

We are moving toward a future where a smartphone can act as a personal health companion. It can help women understand their bodies, notice changes, find reliable information, and have better conversations with healthcare professionals throughout their lives.

Advanced AI, medical research, and more sophisticated digital platforms will speed up this change. But technology by itself won't close the women's health gap. That will take ongoing investment in research, stronger clinical evidence, better access to healthcare, and products built around what women really need.

For investors, the question is no longer whether women's health is a real market. The rising number of femtech companies, their growing user bases, and the investments they attract show that this is a business category that matters more and more.

The bigger question is how many other major healthcare opportunities are still undiscovered simply because we haven't been paying enough attention.

#9723. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9720. Your Retry Logic Might Be the Reason Your System Won't Recover

Gangadharan Venkataraman works on architecture for real-time machine learning and decision platforms.

Gangadharan Venkataraman works on architecture for real-time machine learning and decision platforms.

Gangadharan Venkataraman works on architecture for real-time machine learning and decision platforms.

There is a proverb I grew up with: don’t trouble the trouble, otherwise trouble will trouble you. It’s usually offered as advice about people. It’s even better advice for dealing with distributed systems.

Every engineer shares the same instinct. A call fails. Try it again. It’s such a reasonable response that most frameworks now handle it for you silently, baking in a sensible-looking default of three attempts. You don’t write the retry; you inherit it. For a single client, that’s correct. Networks drop packets. Instances get recycled mid-flight. Trying again is often all it takes. The trouble starts when there are ten thousand clients, and they all have that exact same instinct at the exact same moment.

Imagine a service that comfortably handles 1,000 requests per second with healthy headroom. It can manage about 1,200 before it starts queueing.

Now, something downstream degrades. Not catastrophically—maybe a database failover, an evicted cache node, or a dependency whose p99 latency drifts past the timeout. Responses slow down. Calls start hitting the one-second timeout.

Every caller does what it was configured to do: it retries. Twice.

Every request now times out, meaning every request gets retried again. The load no longer depends on the original fault that started it. The dependency recovers; the service stays down.

Notice what happens to the cause. The original fault—the slow dependency—is no longer what’s generating the traffic. The load is now self-sustaining, feeding entirely on its own response to the fault. You can heal the dependency completely, and the service will stay down because the retry traffic has taken over.

Network engineers gave this a name decades ago: congestion collapse. We tend to rediscover it every time a new layer of the stack gets a default retry policy.

The deeper problem is that a retry is a decision made with insufficient information.

When a caller times out, it knows precisely one thing: no response arrived within the deadline. It doesn't know whether the request was lost in transit, whether it was received and dropped, whether it’s still executing, or whether it actually succeeded while the response is sitting stuck in a buffer somewhere. A timeout isn't a failure signal; it's the absence of a signal—which is an entirely different thing.

So the client guesses. And the guess it makes ("probably transient, try again") is the correct one when the system is healthy, and the exact wrong one when the system is overloaded. Retries are most aggressive precisely when the system can least afford them.

What’s striking about the fixes for this pattern is that none of them involve adding capacity. They are all exercises in restraint:

This dynamic has always mattered, but it matters considerably more now because of what a retry actually costs.

In a conventional service, a wasted retry burns a few milliseconds of CPU and some socket connections. Annoying, but cheap. In an agentic system, a retried step is a full model round trip: tokens in, tokens out, GPU seconds, and the key-value cache held resident for the duration. The amplification factor is identical, but the unit cost has multiplied by orders of magnitude.

It’s worse because agents retry at multiple levels. The orchestration framework retries the failed tool call. Then the model, seeing an error returned in its context window, often decides on its own to try an alternative approach—triggering a secondary retry loop your configuration knows nothing about and cannot bound.

A three-attempt policy wrapped around a model that independently reasons its way into three more attempts is a nine-attempt policy that nobody designed.

If you are running agents in production and haven’t looked at what happens to your token spend during a minor dependency blip, it’s worth an afternoon. The cloud bill is frequently more alarming than the downtime.

The instinct to retry is the instinct to do something. It feels like diligence. When a system struggles, doing something is how we prove we are paying attention.

But a loaded system doesn’t need more attention; it needs less demand. The useful question during a degradation event is almost never "what else can we try?"—it is "what can we stop asking for?"

Shed the traffic, open the breaker, bound the retries, and let the queue drain. More often than not, the system will recover on its own. Leave the trouble alone, and it tends to pass. Poke at it three times a second from ten thousand machines, and it will absolute trouble you back.

I have written about the operational side of this at more length—circuit breakers, backpressure, and the finding that a large share of serious outages begin as a dependency failure that propagates rather than as an internal fault—in Operational Excellence in Real-Time AI Systems, European Journal of Computer Science and Information Technology 13(47), 2025.

Gangadharan Venkataraman works on architecture for real-time machine learning and decision platforms.

#9718. Give Grilled Cheese A Major Flavor And Protein Boost With One Hearty Addition

There are seemingly as many kinds of grilled cheese as there are individuals on this planet. There are, for example, plenty of international styles worth trying, while even the classic all-American versions can consist of a variety of cheeses, like American, cheddar, Gouda, and Havarti. You might like to make yours using mayonnaise on the bread, while your neighbor prefers butter in the pan. And then there are extra fillings and additions. Some people add a little bacon and maple syrup to their sandwiches, while others turn theirs into a breakfast masterpiece with an egg. Another fantastically tasty option is to add chili, which not only imbues the meal with a huge dose of extra flavor, but also gives you a nice protein boost.

Whether you have more leftover chili than you know what to do with, or a can or two in your pantry collecting dust, it's actually the perfect addition. It's savory, hearty, and saucy, which works so well when layered with cheese (which chili often gets topped with) and sandwiched between two slices of bread, pan-browned to crispy perfection. And if you have daily protein goals, a ¼ cup of chili, which is a reasonable starting quantity for a single sandwich, can typically get you roughly 4 to 5 grams closer to meeting that target (though this will vary depending on the recipe).

One of the best things about chili grilled cheese sandwiches is how easy they are to make. You can assemble them in the pan like normal, but add a scoop of chili onto one slice of bread before closing it up. This works well if you're just making one or two sandwiches, but if you have more mouths to feed, you can actually make a whole bunch in the oven at once. You'll just want to be sure to spread butter on the outside of each slice of bread, combine your chili with plenty of shredded cheese to make a gooey, melty filling, and then flip the sandwiches halfway through baking so both sides get nice and toasty.

Now, like all grilled cheeses, this variation is still quite customizable. For example, if you wanted to add some sharpness to help cut through all the richness of the other ingredients, you could sprinkle green onion on top of the chili. Alternatively, if you wanted a bite, plus a bit of spice, sliced or chopped jalapeños would do nicely (or you might make the sweet pickled version known as cowboy candy). To amp up the protein even more, some bacon wouldn't be out of place, either. You could also lean into the idea of a chili cheese dog grilled cheese, and slice a hot dog lengthwise, fry it up, and place that on top of the chili layer.

#9716. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

#9715. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#9713. Skip Butter And Milk: The Canned Ingredient That Makes Burgers Juicier

Juicy burger patties are all about nailing the perfect ratio of fat, moisture, and protein for something that isn't wet or greasy but also isn't dry and crumbly. While butter and milk can certainly help, condensed cream of mushroom soup is a far better and easier alternative that perfectly strikes the balance when you use the right amount.

Cream of mushroom soup may be billed as a shelf-stable meal in its own right, but the condensed version is a canned soup hack for many recipes thanks to its texture and flavor. It's had much of its moisture removed and therefore has a higher ratio of fat. While wet enough to infuse proteins with a bit of juiciness, its fat content helps preserve the tenderness and protect the existing moisture, all with the delicious umami of mushrooms. Condensed varieties also tend to be more potent, so the small amount you'll use for juiciness translates into a subdued but still noticeable taste.

Chopped mushrooms for extra-juicy burgers is an increasingly common tactic, but evenly mixing all the little bits without overworking the meat is challenging. While wet ingredients are far easier to thoroughly disperse, they come with a caveat. You need a starch to hold and release the moisture unless you want it to drip out right away. Breadcrumbs are a common choice in meatballs and other ground beef recipes, and a ratio of half a cup of starch to one 10.5-ounce can to one pound of protein gets the job done quite well.

Burger patties made with condensed cream of mushroom soup are pretty forgiving and more difficult to dry out, but that doesn't mean you can just chuck them on the grill willy-nilly. To preserve the juiciness and keep them easy to work with, you need to know when to leave them alone, whether that's while they're raw, cooking, or resting.

Immediately cooking a burger infused with condensed cream of mushroom soup leaves a lot of surface moisture. This ends up steaming it, so it doesn't develop a good crust and robs it of much of the juice you were attempting to preserve. Letting any patty chill in the fridge helps it firm up and makes it easier to manipulate on the grill, but it also allows the breadcrumbs to absorb the moisture to release later. Similar to marinating, it also helps to let the flavors mix a bit, so you don't end up with pockets of intense mushroom-ness that can ruin an otherwise good bite.

While exact timing varies based on your method, the 5-6-7 rule when cooking burgers is a reliable starting point. Five minutes on one side, six on the other, then seven minutes resting helps you balance enough heat to create a crust with enough time to ensure that the insides are not still raw. The resting is particularly important, as you don't want to release all your juice onto your plate or as steam and make your subsequent bites drier.

#9712. RabbitMQ on Kubernetes: Fixing “Failed to create dirty CPU scheduler thread” (Error 11)

We deploy RabbitMQ across single-node and three-node Kubernetes clusters in both staging and production environments to enable asynchronous messaging across our microservices architecture. High availability and predictable message queuing are critical to keeping our downstream processing pipelines operational.

A few weeks back, our infrastructure and SRE teams ran into a frustrating crash loop on one of our high-availability RabbitMQ statefulsets. RabbitMQ liveness probes kept failing randomly and repeatedly, throwing severe thread creation errors into the kubelet logs and causing unexpected pod restarts.

We observed this issue in at least five deployments. The measurements described in this article were collected with RabbitMQ 3.13.3 and Erlang/OTP 26; CPU limits, PID limits, and scheduler counts can differ across deployments.

When inspecting the cluster logs, we repeatedly observed the following log entries emitting from the pod container:

To begin troubleshooting, we analyzed the root mechanics of the system call error. In standard Linux error definitions (errno.h), Error 11 maps directly to EAGAIN (Resource temporarily unavailable). When emitted during process creation via fork() or thread creation via pthread_create(), EAGAIN indicates that the OS kernel or execution context refused to allocate a new task because a configured resource limit was reached.

In containerized environments, this error typically points to one of three underlying system constraints:

Our Kubernetes cluster nodes enforce a default pod PID limit of 1024 (podPIDsLimit: 1024). Our initial hypothesis was that the combined workload inside the RabbitMQ pod was breaching this limit and exhausting available task IDs.

To test this hypothesis systematically, we logged into the running container to check standard user limits:

Because ulimit -u reported unlimited inside the container user namespace, standard POSIX limits were not enforcing the block. However, we

still needed a controlled method to verify whether the container environment was hitting cgroup enforced process cap under execution.

We authored a lightweight bash script (eat_pid.sh) designed to rapidly spawn background sub-processes and hold them open:

We executed ./eat_pid.sh 1000 inside the container, script failed almost immediately with the error: fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable. Concurrently, the RabbitMQ runtime threw the exact same log: Failed to create dirty CPU scheduler thread 138, error = 11,

The stress test reproduced EAGAIN when the pod approached its configured PID ceiling. Together with the probe-correlated thread spikes and the improvement after disabling the probes, this supports PID pressure as the likely cause in this environment. A contemporaneous reading of pids.current and pids.max during an incident would provide direct confirmation of the cgroup limit.

Having validated that thread exhaustion was occurring, our next step was determining which process inside the container was consuming hundreds of tasks. We opened an interactive session inside the pod and monitored active threads in real time:

While observing the task list, we noticed distinct thread spikes occurring every 30 seconds. This 30-second interval matched our RabbitMQ liveness and readiness probe configurations exactly under our initial deployment setup, the health probes executed shell-based rabbitmqctl CLI commands (such as rabbitmqctl status or rabbitmqctl ping) inside the container.

To isolate the probes, we temporarily disabled the liveness and readiness definitions in the pod spec and monitored the baseline thread count. Without the probes, thread allocation flattened into a completely stable baseline. Re-enabling the probes caused immediate thread spikes. The health checks were unambiguously responsible for the task accumulation.

We needed to profile rabbitmqctl to quantify its exact system call behavior and understand why a basic status check generated massive thread spikes. We used strace to count clone() system calls during a single invocation.

These calls create tasks; the count is useful for comparing runs, but it does not by itself identify every task as an Erlang scheduler thread:

The trace counted more than 700 clone() system calls for one rabbitmqctl invocation in this test. Across the node types we tested, the clone() count increased with the logical CPU capacity visible to the CLI VM. This observation is specific to the tested RabbitMQ/Erlang image and container CPU configuration.

Understanding Erlang OTP Scheduler Mechanics

To understand why a simple CLI utility requires 700 system calls, it helps to examine the internal architecture of the Erlang Runtime System (ERTS), rabbitmqctl is not a self-contained compiled binary (like a Go or C executable). It is an Erlang application wrapper. Launching rabbitmqctl boots an entire Erlang VM instance inside the container.

By default, the Erlang VM is designed for high-concurrency server workloads and automatically optimizes itself for multi-core hardware. When ERTS initializes, it inspects the operating system to count physical/logical CPU cores and automatically initializes three distinct pools of native OS scheduler threads:

This auto-scaling behavior creates a severe architectural friction point inside Kubernetes.

Container runtimes share the underlying host kernel. Unless explicitly restricted at the application runtime layer, Erlang inspects /proc/cpuinfo or host cgroups and detects all CPU cores available on the physical worker node (e.g. 32, 64, or 128 cores), completely ignoring CPU request/limit throttles assigned to the container.

As a result, on a 32-core node, executing rabbitmqctl attempts to initialize 32 Normal Schedulers, 32 Dirty CPU Schedulers, a large Dirty I/O pool, and supporting VM management threads.

When Kubernetes triggers liveness and readiness probes concurrently every few seconds, multiple rabbitmqctl instances run simultaneously alongside the main RabbitMQ server daemon (beam.smp). Combined, these short-lived VMs spawn hundreds of threads, breaching the pod's 1024 PID cap and causing pthread_create to fail with error = 11.

Standard RabbitMQ documentation does not prominently detail CLI thread tuning. However, inspecting the Erlang startup wrapper scripts for rabbitmqctl revealed an environment variable designed for runtime customization: RABBITMQ_CTL_ERL_ARGS.

By defining RABBITMQ_CTL_ERL_ARGS, we can pass explicit Erlang VM startup flags to every rabbitmqctl invocation without altering the thread settings of the primary RabbitMQ server.

We configured the following VM restriction flags:

We exported the configuration inside the container environment:

After exporting the environment variable, we re-ran strace against rabbitmqctl:

The results were immediate: clone() system calls dropped from ~700 down to just 8 per invocation. Total thread consumption remained negligible, eliminating probe-induced crashes and stabilizing pod execution.

1: Configure RABBITMQ_CTL_ERL_ARGS in Pod Manifests

Include RABBITMQ_CTL_ERL_ARGS="+S 1:1 +SDcpu 1:1 +SDio 1:1" in your StatefulSet environment definitions if your health checks rely on CLI utilities:

2. Account for Host-Level Multi-Core Scaling

Be aware that runtimes like Erlang, Java (JVM), and Node.js often auto-detect host physical cores rather than container limits. Always restrict thread pools explicitly in containerized environments.

Whenever possible, replace CLI exec probes (rabbitmqctl) with native HTTP probes pointing to the RabbitMQ Management Plugin (port 15672). HTTP health checks execute against the existing server process and eliminate subprocess fork overhead entirely. RabbitMQ’s HTTP API requires authentication. Configure probe access using a secure method supported by your deployment, and do not put credentials directly in a plain-text manifest. Verify that these endpoints are available in the RabbitMQ version you run.
