#9710. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

Note: This article contains affiliate links, meaning we make a small commission if you buy any premium plan from our link.

#9709. The Creamy Ingredient That Makes PB&J Sandwiches 10x More Delicious

When you want to upgrade your peanut butter and jelly sandwich, you don't have to splurge on high-priced bread or get particular about the jam like Ina Garten. How you prepare it can make all the difference, and treating it like a grilled cheese with a bit of butter on the outside can give you a serious result with even more serious flavor.

Toasting the exterior of your sandwich with butter in a pan gives you a golden-brown outside packed with richness and flavor. It brings out the best in your bread and warms the peanut butter and jelly for something as gooey as melted cheese but infinitely creamier. This is especially true if you use a top-ranked store-bought butter brand, since even a small amount acts like a seasoning and truly upgrades the whole thing. The toasted bread and melted insides create a dichotomy of textures that transforms one of the simplest recipes in the world into something more decadent and complex.

While the heat won't caramelize the sugars in the jelly or toast the peanut butter fats, it does make them taste more delicious. Smell is just as important as taste when enjoying a meal, and heat releases those aromas so you can enjoy them more. This is especially nice if you work with higher-end, complex ingredients like artisan jellies, as it lets you better experience each little nuance.

A new preparation method means new opportunities for better flavor. While simple toasting alone is enough to make any mixture of ingredients delicious, taking inspiration from other recipes and choosing the right type of bread maximizes that effect.

While you should avoid crusty bread for a PB&J because it tends to be a bit dry, this trick is a great way of getting around that. Even older bread gets a texture boost, transforming it from stale and brittle to crispy and delicious. If you're focusing on the rich, buttery flavor, using something full of dips and ridges, like sourdough or a rustic country-style loaf, only lets you use more butter for a thoroughly flavored exterior. Just be sure not to use something with deep holes that your filling can leak through, as it may burn in the pan and foul the flavor.

If you want to take things even further, you can make the most decadent PB&J French toast with this method. It's especially great if you dip a soft, fluffy white bread or brioche in the egg mixture, giving you something that's pillowy on the inside and crispy on the outside. Butter alone can toast the bread, but the addition of milk and eggs adds binding proteins and delicious fats that create a stronger, but still crispy, structure that holds its shape well and prevents the liquidy insides from oversaturating the bread.

#9706. Engineering Zero-State Search

I am an Engineering leader with over 15+ years experience building multi billion user, large scale, low latency and ML driven monetization

I am an Engineering leader with over 15+ years experience building multi billion user, large scale, low latency and ML driven monetization

I am an Engineering leader with over 15+ years experience building multi billion user, large scale, low latency and ML driven monetization

Open Spotify, Netflix, or almost any modern delivery app, and tap the search bar. Before you type a single letter, the screen is already full. You see recent genres, trending queries, categories tailored to the time of day, or items you lingered on yesterday.

In information retrieval, this is the zero-state search.

Traditional search engines are reactive. They wait for a text string, parse tokens, hit an inverted index or vector store, and rank candidates against explicit intent. zero-state search flips that sequence. The ranking decision happens before the user expresses any intent at all.

That shift sounds like a minor UI convenience, but it changes the underlying systems problem. When you populate a search screen ahead of the first keystroke, you are trading explicit intent for latency and convenience. Get it right, and the user saves five seconds of typing. Get it wrong, and you have built a high-speed wall of stale, repetitive guesses that gets in the way of actual search.

Here is how the engineering problem changes when ranking moves ahead of the query—and why standard offline relevance metrics usually fail to catch the worst UX bugs.

When a user taps into a search bar, your latency budget is unforgiving. If  zero-state suggestions take 400ms to pop in, the user has already started typing, and the UI jump when the suggestions finally render will cause mis-taps. To feel native, zero-state payloads need to resolve in under 50ms to 100ms—often served straight from a local device cache or an edge key-value store.

Because you cannot run heavy multi-stage ranking at tap time, the work moves earlier. Candidate generation and scoring happen asynchronously: in nightly batch jobs, on app launch, or triggered by background event streams.

Precomputation buys you speed, but it creates an immediate freshness problem.

Suppose a user spends twenty minutes browsing hiking boots on an e-commerce app, buys a pair, and closes the app. If your  zero-state pipeline relies on a batch job that recomputes user embeddings every six hours, the next time that user taps the search bar, your system will proudly suggest hiking boots. The prediction had a high offline probability score, but in the real world, the task is over.

To make precomputed rankings work without feeling broken, teams usually have to split the scoring pipeline into two layers:

The Slow Layer (Batch/Nearline): Computes broad affinity scores, collaborative filtering candidates, and long-term category preferences. This populates the candidate pool.

The Fast Re-ranker (Edge/Client-side): Applies lightweight, deterministic rules at read time. It checks local session state, filters out items purchased or dismissed in the last ten minutes, and adjusts weights based on immediate context (like time of day or device connection).

If you only build the slow layer, your app will feel like it has amnesia about what the user just did.

The most common mistake in  zero-state ranking is reusing the exact same objective function used for standard search or home-feed click-through rate (CTR).

When a user types "wireless mechanical keyboard", narrowing the results to ten nearly identical keyboards is a win. You have an explicit constraint. Before a query, you have no constraint. If your model notices a user clicked on Italian restaurants twice last week and responds by filling every slot on the  zero-state screen with pasta places, you haven't built a discovery tool. You've built a rut.

High pointwise scores do not equal a useful screen. If five candidates each have a 15% probability of being clicked, but all five represent the exact same intent cluster, showing all five wastes four slots.

Instead of pure relevance sorting, zero-state ranking has to be treated as a portfolio optimization problem (or a slated recommendation problem). The goal isn't for every item on the screen to be right; the goal is for at least one item on the screen to match the user's unspoken mood.

In practice, this requires a few structural guardrails in the ranking logic:

Intent Clustering & Deduplication: Group candidates by semantic category or task before final slot allocation. Cap how many slots any single cluster can claim, regardless of raw model score.

Impression Decay (Fatigue Penalties): If a user has seen a  zero-state suggestion three times across three sessions and ignored it every time, its score should decay aggressively. Without impression discounting, static high-prior items (like a user's all-time top genre) will squat on the top slot forever.

Dedicated Exploration Slots: Reserve 10% to 20% of the visible real estate for low-confidence, high-variance candidates or trending global queries. If you never show anything outside the user's historical profile, the model can only reinforce its own past predictions.

Every proactive recommendation carries an implicit risk: it is a guess made on the user's behalf, and most of the time, guesses miss.

When a recommendation misses on a passive browse feed, the cost is low—the user just keeps scrolling. When a recommendation misses on a search screen, the user is often trying to accomplish a specific task. If your  zero-state interface hijacks the screen, pushes the keyboard down, or requires an extra tap to clear a pre-filled suggestion, a wrong guess actively slows the user down.

Good  zero-state systems are designed to be ignored at zero cost.

That means the boundary between "browsing suggestions" and "typing a query" has to be frictionless. The text cursor should be focused and ready. The moment the first character is typed, the  zero-state state should yield immediately to prefix autocomplete without layout lag. Users shouldn't have to fight the system's prediction to state their actual intent.

How do you know if your  zero-state ranking is actually helping users, rather than just farming accidental taps?

Looking at the click-through rate on the  zero-state screen in isolation is a trap. You can easily inflate zero-state CTR by making the suggestion cards huge, hiding the keyboard by default, or showing clickbait trending topics. Your  zero-state metrics will go up while overall search satisfaction tanks.

Engineers working on pre-query systems should evaluate the entire session trajectory, not just the first tap:

Downstream Task Completion (Assisted Success): When a user clicks a  zero-state suggestion, do they actually complete a downstream action (play a song, read an article, add to cart), or do they immediately bounce back to the search bar and type a manual query? A click followed by an immediate back-navigation within 3 seconds is a false positive.

Time-to-Success: Compare sessions that start with a  zero-state tap against sessions that start with manual typing. Does the precomputed screen actually reduce the time it takes for a user to find something they engage with?

Query Reformulation & Abandonment Rate: If introducing a new  zero-state ranking model increases the rate at which users abandon the search tab entirely, your suggestions are likely creating visual noise or decision fatigue.

Slot Entropy / Refresh Rate: Measure how often the top N slots actually change for a given user across consecutive sessions. If your jaccard similarity between Tuesday's screen and Wednesday's screen is 0.95, your freshness signals are under-weighted.

Moving ranking ahead of the first keystroke doesn't replace search. Plenty of users open an app knowing the exact string they want to type, and the best thing a system can do for them is stay out of the way.

But for the users who open search with a half-formed goal—looking for something to watch, something to eat, or a topic they were researching yesterday—the  zero-state screen is where retrieval actually begins. Treating that screen as a first-class systems problem means looking past raw prediction scores. It requires balancing precomputed speed with real-time session context, penalizing repetition, and designing an interface that lets the user overrule the algorithm without missing a beat.

The Millisecond Conundrum: Balancing Latency, Freshness, and Intelligence at Scale

#9705. This Chain Was Dunkin's Bitter Rival In The '50s — Now It's The Most Popular Donut Spot In Japan

Dunkin' is one of America's favorite spots to grab a quick donut and one of its famous syrup-infused iced coffees — which we ranked from worst to best. Today, the chain boasts more than 10,000 stores in the U.S. alone and sits comfortably at the top of the country's donut hierarchy. However, it wasn't always the undisputed heavyweight. In a rivalry that gives McDonald's and Burger King a run for their money, Dunkin' spent decades going head-to-head with Mister Donut. Ultimately, Dunkin' came out on top — at least, if we're talking strictly about the USA. Over in Japan, Mister Donut reigns supreme.

What makes this feud particularly fascinating is that it was a family affair. Dunkin', originally known as Dunkin' Donuts, was founded in 1950 by William Rosenberg. The simple combination of donuts and coffee proved to be a huge success. Naturally, Rosenberg wanted to expand the business through franchising. So far, so good, right? Well, not everyone was happy with the idea, including Harry Winokur, Rosenberg's brother-in-law. In a move that would spark a decades-long rivalry, Winokur left the business and opened Mister Donut just a few miles from Dunkin's original location. He even embraced franchising, with Mister Donut employees reportedly being prohibited from saying the word "dunk" in their stores.

As is often the case, feuds rarely end with a clear winner. In 1990, Dunkin' acquired Mister Donut and rebranded nearly all of its American locations as Dunkin' stores (ouch). Today, just one Mister Donut location remains in the U.S. That must have been a hit on Winokur's pride, but while Dunkin' was busy making cereal in the '80s, Mister Donut was thriving on the other side of the world. Today, Mister Donut is Japan's leading donut chain, with more than 900 locations in operation.

Japan has embraced plenty of Western-style foods with open arms. Think of the juicy, hamburger-inspired hambāgu, or comforting pizza toast with its wide array of toppings. Mister Donut also happens to fit comfortably into this category. However, one thing worth knowing about Japan's take on Western staples is that they're rarely direct copies. Instead, the country has a knack for putting its own spin on imported dishes. That's exactly how Mister Donut managed to carve out a place for itself in the market.

The first Mister Donut opened its doors in Japan in 1971, after business executive Seiichi Suzuki acquired the exclusive rights to operate the brand in the country. The original menu featured familiar American favorites, but Suzuki also introduced items and adjustments designed to appeal to local tastes. These included reducing the sugar content of certain products, serving more modest portions, and creating a cozy, sit-down atmosphere. The approach proved successful, and Mister Donut quickly expanded across Japan. Dunkin', meanwhile, had also tried its luck in the Japanese market, opening its first location in 1970. While Mister Donut continued to grow, Dunkin' struggled to gain a foothold and eventually left Japan altogether in 1998.

In 1989, Suzuki's company Duskin acquired full ownership of Mister Donut's Japanese operations, giving it greater freedom to develop the brand's distinctly Japanese identity. From there, the chain continued to expand, eventually bringing its donuts to markets including Thailand, Australia, Taiwan, and Singapore. Today, Mister Donut is best known for its playful, distinctly Japanese creations, particularly the Pon De Ring, a chewy, ring-shaped donut made up of small dough balls, and Mocchurin, its mochi-inspired donut line that is so soft, they require paper trays to keep each donut from losing its shape.

#9702. Skip Tortilla Chips: Make Totchos For 10x The Flavor & Texture

The appeal of nachos is easy to understand: Cover tortilla chips with a variable mix of cheese, meat, and beans, and dig into a mouth-watering textural experience. It's a dish concept that originated in Mexico, but it has since become widely popularized in the USA, welcoming many modifications in the process. Want a version with a thick boost in flavor and texture? Make a batch of totchos, swapping the tortilla chips for miniature hash browns (aka tater tots).

At first glance, it may seem like potatoes and nacho toppings shouldn't go together; tots are often a breakfast dish, after all. Yet the spuds make for an excellent starchy flavor canvas, ready for whatever nacho fixings you throw on. Like other loaded tater tot recipes, it's all about contrasting flavors atop a canvas of crispy potatoes.

So layer on ingredients like gooey cheese, corn and beans, flavorful ground meat or chorizo, salsa, pickled jalapeños, and more. Some bites will get a little wet, but most will remain crunchy. Yet since tater tots are much thicker than chips, the underside retains a sturdy foundation, propping up a nacho twist with a little more heft. It's among the most delicious hacks for a bag of frozen tater tots, meshing together a freezer classic item with a crowd favorite formula.

A platter of totchos fits a variety of contexts. Layer on an abundance of festive components, and the dish can be an all-out party platter. Keep it to a simple meat and cheese, and you get an affordable and comforting rendition. Whichever route you go for, construct the dish with a few considerations in mind to optimize both flavor and texture.

When preparing the tater tots, aim for peak crunch, so cook them well before you add your toppings. A hot oven gets the job done, but consider also using the air fryer for restaurant-level crunch, or even pan-frying the tots — maybe even in chorizo fat for added flavor. Next in importance is how to incorporate the dairy, another nacho cornerstone.

If you're making a liquidy nacho cheese sauce, you can simply drizzle the condiment onto your tots. However, if you're using shredded cheese, you'll want to melt the component on top of the tots in the oven for around five minutes. During this step, you can include already prepped ground beef taco meat, too, melding the dish components alongside the bed of potatoes.

Only right before serving should you include cold ingredients. Keep it simple with chopped lettuce and onions, a light drizzle of sour cream or crema, or consider something more complex, like pico de gallo and guacamole. Cilantro and scallions are always welcome, as is a squeeze of lime. Dig in with a fork and knife (and we do suggest using cutlery — unlike with chips, you won't be easily able to grab individual tots); totchos's hearty appeal is immediate — it's the magic of nachos, with a heftier base.

#9701. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

#9698. How Foreign Businesses Can Accept UPI Payments and Subscriptions in India

India has one of the world’s largest digital audiences - and a payment environment that can punish assumptions imported from the United States or Europe. A checkout that supports international cards may technically accept a payment from India, but that does not mean it fits how a typical Indian customer prefers to pay. The opportunity is not simply to display prices in rupees. It is to choose the right rail, authorization experience, commercial partner, and renewal architecture.

UPI deserves to be treated as a first-class option, not because cards are irrelevant, but because a card-only strategy can unnecessarily limit reach. Equally important: accepting a one-time UPI payment is not the same as making recurring UPI billing work for a foreign merchant. The distinction is where a large part of the engineering effort begins.

India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) handled 241.62 billion transactions worth approximately ₹314.23 lakh crore in FY2025-26, according to a government release drawing on NPCI data. The number of transactions was around five times the FY2021-22 level. By June 2026, roughly 554.9 million users had been onboarded to UPI.

These figures tell us that UPI has achieved extraordinary breadth; they do not, by themselves, prove its conversion rate for an online subscription checkout. UPI transaction totals span different use cases, including transfers between individuals and payments to merchants. Comparing every UPI transaction with only credit-card purchase transactions would be an apples-to-oranges comparison. The relevant question for a seller is narrower: how much of its own target audience can pay successfully, and how readily, with each method?

That distinction matters. A foreign business does not need to replace cards completely. It should test whether adding UPI to a well-designed checkout increases payment completion among its intended Indian customers, without compromising subscription operations or compliance.

A credit card is a convenient default for many American subscription products. In India, it is a less universal starting point. Credit cards depend on issuer underwriting and access to a line of credit. RBI directions require issuers to assess an applicant's credit risk with reference to their independent financial means. Cards in circulation are also not the same as distinct people who hold an active, usable card.

The problem is both availability and checkout readiness. RBI card-security rules require cards to be issued with domestic ATM and point-of-sale use enabled as the baseline, while cardholders can control online and international transaction settings. An Indian customer may have a card yet be unable to complete a cross-border, card-not-present transaction until they change issuer settings. That failure can look like an ordinary declined payment to the merchant.

Preference also matters, but it deserves more careful language than a national stereotype. UPI’s familiarity, immediate account-based payment experience, wide merchant acceptance, and lack of a revolving credit requirement can make it appealing to customers who have access to both methods. Rather than assume all Indian consumers dislike credit, businesses should measure customer preferences, available instruments, authorization success and payment-method selection in their own funnel.

The market is connected, but willingness to pay varies widely. TRAI reports approximately 1.09 billion internet subscriptions as of March 2026. The FICCI-EY analysis estimates that Indian digital-subscription revenue grew 60% to ₹163 billion in calendar 2025, including video, audio and news. Within video, its estimates show 216 million paid subscriptions across 143 million households, many accessed through bundled offers.

These numbers demonstrate growth and market diversity; they should not be used to infer that the average paid video subscription costs ₹63 a month. The ₹163 billion revenue total covers more than video, the 216 million count refers to video subscriptions, and bundles complicate the relationship between subscriptions and what end users pay directly. A headline blended “price” created by dividing those incompatible figures would be misleading.

For a foreign merchant, pricing solely in dollars may mean a foreign-currency card purchase, possible issuer conversion fees, and a price on the statement that differs from the amount shown at checkout. The exact cost depends on the card, issuer and transaction arrangement. Card restrictions can also affect payment success. INR pricing paired with a viable local collection flow can reduce those sources of customer friction, but the business still needs to account for local taxes, foreign exchange and settlement costs within its own economics.

The practical takeaway: build the Indian price from customer value, competition, tax treatment, and payment economics. Do not calculate it solely by multiplying a US list price by the spot exchange rate.

UPI is an interoperable, real-time payment system operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). A customer typically initiates or approves a payment in a UPI-enabled app linked to their bank account. The merchant and its payment partners receive a transaction result, while bank-account identifiers need not be entered on the merchant’s checkout page. It is more accurate to say the account credential is not exposed to the merchant than to say no credential or identifying information ever travels through the payment network.

A merchant can present an app-intent link on mobile or a QR-based flow on desktop; a collect flow may also be supported depending on the provider and use case. Availability, customer prompts, and conversion vary by product and UPI app. The only reliable way to pick the checkout UX is to test the actual payment paths, including app switches, slow callbacks, user cancellations and return-to-merchant behavior.

Historically, bank-account-funded UPI merchant transactions operated largely under a zero-MDR framework. A September 2026 announcement set out a 0.4% merchant discount rate (MDR) for eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 or more. Person-to-person transfers, payments of ₹2,000 or less, and qualifying small-merchant transactions remain exempt; some sectors have lower or flat rates.

For subscription businesses, one-time checkout and recurring collection need to be distinguished. NPCI’s policy FAQ expressly states that automated recurring standing instructions (UPI AutoPay mandates), including OTT subscriptions, do not attract the prescribed MDR. This exemption concerns the network MDR; it should not be mistaken for a guarantee that gateways, aggregators, or cross-border providers will charge no processing, settlement, or foreign-exchange fees.

The announced rates were initially scheduled for October 15, 2026, but NPCI deferred the rollout until after Diwali. As of November 13, 2026, no replacement effective date had been confirmed. MDR is a merchant-acceptance cost, not an extra UPI checkout surcharge to the customer. Merchants should confirm the effective date, applicable transaction classifications including mandate renewals and their actual provider fee schedule and net settlement with the acquiring or aggregation partner. Broad claims that UPI is always free for merchants, or that the new 0.4% MDR already applies to all UPI payments, are misleading.

For subscriptions, UPI AutoPay adds an electronic mandate. The customer authorizes its setup, and later debit attempts are made against that mandate subject to network, bank, regulatory and mandate-specific rules. The payment provider - not the merchant alone implements the network interactions; the merchant must still maintain the correct business state.

Under RBI’s Digital Payments – E-mandate Framework, 2026, recurring transactions up to ₹15,000 generally may proceed without additional authentication after mandate setup; higher authentication-free thresholds apply to specified categories such as insurance, mutual funds and credit-card bills. Issuers generally must send a pre-debit notification at least 24 hours before charging, subject to stated exceptions. This requires advance scheduling and coordination; it does not mean that every same-day debit is prohibited or that a merchant should blindly charge a day early.

The critical architecture distinction is that subscription state and mandate state are independent. A subscription may remain active in the product database after a customer pauses or revokes the payment mandate in their UPI app. A mandate may be valid when the renewal request is created but fail during execution. Every renewal needs its own attempt, result, retries and reconciliation against the authoritative provider events.

A foreign business has several possible entry models: an Indian entity collecting locally, an arrangement with an Indian payment aggregator and a compliant cross-border settlement path, or a merchant-of-record (MoR) service that contracts with the end customer as seller. These models differ materially in who sells the product, who owns tax and refunds, whose name appears on the customer’s statement, where funds settle, and who handles disputes.

Do not assume that registering a foreign merchant with a globally known processor automatically enables Indian UPI collection. Nor is a locally incorporated subsidiary the only theoretical route. RBI’s Payment Aggregator–Cross Border (PA-CB) framework regulates entities facilitating import and export payments. The actual permissible configuration depends on the authorized entities and their arrangements.

A processor’s brand name is less important than the regulated entity providing the service. Ask the provider for the legal entity name, its relevant RBI authorization, the cross-border direction in which the payment is classified, the bank/settlement chain and the specific supported merchant category. The “inward” and “outward” labels can be confusing if read from the foreign seller’s point of view: check the RBI definitions and the exact transaction flow rather than guessing from a label.

Licensing does not itself establish product availability. A provider may be authorized for cross-border collection yet offer UPI only to certain industries, currencies, checkout integrations or one-time transactions. Ask explicitly whether one-time UPI, mandate registration and renewal debits are enabled for a foreign-registered business in your category. Examples of published provider documentation for cross-border UPI mandates now exist, including PayU’s cross-border UPI consent flow and Paddle’s UPI AutoPay offering; eligibility and contracting still need confirmation.

For recurring billing, obtain the answers before integration: Does the provider offer mandate registration, cancellation, pause, and status queries? Who sends the pre-debit notice? What time windows and retry limits apply? Which transaction results are final, and which are pending? How do asynchronous provider webhooks map to subscription, invoice, and entitlement states? What recovery experience is available after mandate revocation?

Store mandates as separate records linked to subscriptions; make debit and webhook processing idempotent; reconcile transaction IDs with the provider; handle delayed and reversed results; and provide a card or alternative-method recovery path when AutoPay is unavailable. Do not mark an invoice paid merely because the mandate exists or the debit request was accepted.

Digital supplies to Indian consumers may create Indian GST obligations, including under rules for online information and database access or retrieval (OIDAR) services. The responsible party depends on the transaction and seller-of-record structure. Tax obligations do not vanish because the payment uses UPI or because a third party processes funds. Have an India-qualified tax adviser validate the specific service, customer types and contractual arrangements.

Your margin model should separately account for INR list price, applicable tax, provider and settlement fees, currency conversion, chargebacks or disputes where relevant, refunds and payment-recovery expenses. Even with a simple consumer-facing checkout, the underlying economics are not automatically simple.

Consider a digital publisher offering a US subscription at $12 per month. The first launch uses an international-card checkout with dollar pricing. A later, localized experiment offers ₹999 per month, displays the applicable tax treatment clearly, supports eligible local payment methods, and routes UPI through a provider that has confirmed this merchant’s contract and product eligibility.

The ₹999 figure is intentionally illustrative - not a foreign-exchange conversion, market benchmark, or actual business result. The real decision would require price research and controlled testing. The operational differences are more important than the numbers:

USD price; issuer FX may affect statement amount

INR price; taxes and merchant FX/settlement modeled

Cards plus approved UPI flow; app/QR UX tested

Card credential/network token and card rules

UPI AutoPay only where contractually supported; mandate state tracked

Revoked or failed mandates, fallback payments and explicit reauthorization

Checkout starts and accepted card charges

Net paid conversion, first renewal, recovered revenue and support burden

What would prove the strategy works? Not UPI’s national market share. Measure paid checkout conversion by payment method, first-cycle authorization success, the proportion of customers able to register recurring mandates, renewal collection rate after 30 and 60 days, net realized revenue, refund/support cost, and payment-method fallback. Segment those metrics by app, device, acquisition channel, and price cohort.

UPI is not a logo to add next to Visa and Mastercard. It changes the customer’s payment behavior, the merchant’s collection choices and, for recurring revenue, the authorization model itself. But the case for UPI should not be overstated: national transaction totals are not a merchant conversion study, not every foreign seller can activate every UPI product, and fee policy is evolving.

The right approach is to combine local pricing research, a compliant collection chain, carefully tested UPI and card experiences, and an architecture that treats mandates as live customer-controlled permissions. Real localization means adapting the payment architecture to the market - not merely translating the price into its currency.

Author’s note: Sources for the original article were checked on 19 October 2026. Inline source links and the merchant-fee section were reviewed and updated on 13 November 2026. Provider capabilities, fees, and regulations can change; confirm them again before launching. This article is business and engineering analysis, not legal or tax advice.

#9696. 11 Best Classic American Candy Stores Across The US

There's hardly a saying that expresses unbridled joy like "kid in a candy store." But why do kids get all the fun? Candy stores, those brightly colored meccas of sky-high sugar intake, beckon many Americans far into adulthood. Candy, after all, is one of those food products that can really take us back, so candy stores are capable of injecting a sense of nostalgia, childlike reverie, and excitement into anyone's day.

Candy has long been a staple of American culture, with the oldest candy stores in the United States stretching back into past centuries. In the modern world, however, candy enthusiasts keep tabs on their favorite indulgences through candy-focused blogs, sweets-obsessed Instagram accounts, and TikTok viral candy sensations. Meanwhile, towns, states, and even nationwide publications regularly hold contests for the best candy store in the area (or in the country). These sources, and more, inspired this list of the coolest candy stores in the United States.

And in a society where more is more, candy stores have evolved from quaint little shops (still worth a visit for transporting yourself to the past) to mega-sized outlets overflowing with sweets. Some have blossomed into department store-level or warehouse-like square footage, others have added attractions far beyond the candy itself, from mini golf to candy museums, and some are just old-time-tastic. The candy stores listed here are not just the perfect places to get your candy fix. They've become must-visit destinations for travelers around the country.

Philadelphia's Shane Confectionery is one of America's oldest candy stores — in fact, it's the oldest continuously operated confectionery. The company emphasizes that this claim to fame means that its operation has been consistently making and selling confections longer than any other site in America, in a historic four-story brick building that's survived for over 150 years.

But it wasn't until 1910, when the company was sold to Edward R. Shane, that many of the retail shop's intricate, old-fashioned design elements were put into place. As the company explains, Shane installed elaborately carved cabinets, curved glass showcases, and marble countertops to highlight his confections, as well as stained glass transom windows above the storefront to allure passersby in front of his shop. Best of all, many of these architectural details have been restored and are on display in the shop today, making a visit there a bit like stepping into a charming bygone era.

It's no wonder that Eater Philadelphia has called Shane Confectionery the "time portal to Philadelphia's sugary past," calling out the efforts of current owners, brothers Ryan and Eric Berley, who breathed new life into the longstanding business in 2011. Fans regularly show it love online as a must-visit when living in or traveling through the City of Brotherly Love.

With enthusiastic reviews and a high rankings online, Sweet Pete's Candy in Jacksonville, Florida, is hailed as the largest candy store in the Southeast. And the setting can't be beat: Visit Jacksonville points out that it's located in a historic 22,000-square-foot mansion right in the heart of downtown. From sour candies to hand-pulled lollipops, Sweet Pete's has your candy cravings covered.

Sweet Pete's Candy also gets a leg up on the candy competition by serving customers with dietary restrictions. It offers an entire allergy-friendly array of candies, including a selection of gluten-free, dairy-free, vegan-friendly, and nut-free options. A classic treat is Pete's Famous Sea Salt Caramel, now available in different flavors, like Apple Pie.

Meanwhile, visitors can make a day out of their visit, because Sweet Pete's also houses Fizzies & Fare, an in-house restaurant and bar that's touted by the company as home to hundreds of unique craft sodas, over-the-top Crazy Shakes, classic American eats, candy-inspired cocktails, and more. Candy fans can also learn how their favorite candies are made through a guided tour, led by one of the staff's "Candy Connoisseurs," through the three-story "candy mansion," then grab their own handmade custom chocolate bar fresh from Sweet Pete's kitchen. The business even hosts parties, events, field trips for local school kids, and classes on-site.

Sweet Mickey's, in the Ballard neighborhood of Seattle, is named after owner Randy Brinker's grandma and pays homage to her bygone party shop and homemade sweets. Many publications laud it as one of the best candy stores in the country, thanks to its variety of homemade fudges and truffles alongside classic candy favorites like Sugar Babies and international sensations like Danish salted licorice.

With a storefront tucked into the charming brick buildings of historic Ballard, it's the perfect place for a candy store with a vintage vibe and an old-time Americana aesthetic. From handmade goodies to its carefully curated selection of traditional and artisanal sweets from around the globe, candy lovers (or even the pickiest of eaters) can find something for them.

Even better, this candy store has a heart. Since its 2012 grand opening, it has supported the local Little League, sponsored movie nights in the park, and hosted onsite parties and events to create sweet memories and build community.

It'Sugar, with candy-colored locations nationwide, was already known for its San Francisco flagship location, with a three-floor candy store in Fisherman's Wharf. The brand, with locations from coast to coast, then opened a 24,000-square-foot location in East Rutherford, New Jersey's American Dream shopping mall. This location, dubbed the World's First Candy Department Store, also spans three floors, though there are plenty across the country.

Some of its over-the-top features at the East Rutherford location include: a three-story-tall Statue of Liberty replica covered in more than 1.5 million Jelly Belly beans, an immersive lollipop garden filled with nearly 10,000 lollipops, dozens of branded shops like Sour Patch Kids, Swedish Fish, Nerds, Starburst, and Reese's. It's truly a candy lover's dream come true. YouTubers have hailed it as an amazing feat of candy awesomeness, all a stone's throw from New York City.

The brand It'Sugar calls itself a "retailtainer," a mashup of retailer and entertainment. As company lore explains, the brand was founded by candy veteran Jeff Rubin in 2006 and has grown to more than 120 locations throughout the United States and Canada. It's known for "absurd sugar innovations" and the Sugar High Club, with which loyal visitors can earn points for their purchases — then, of course, they can cash them in for more sugar.

Cleveland hosts North America's largest candy store, going strong for more than 75 years: b.a. Sweetie Candy Company. Cleveland.com calls it Cleveland's version of Willy Wonka's Candy Factory, and for good reason. Company stats boast that it hosts more than 500,000 visitors per year (making it one of the city's top attractions) and stocks more than 5,500 items in its wholesale store, to the tune of over $5 million in inventory on-hand at any given time.

With classic candy, retro candy, bulk candy, wholesale candy, and more, the store promises "the absolute largest variety of candy available anywhere in North America." Meaning, if you need 1,000 pounds of Tootsie Rolls to throw a parade, it's your outlet. It even keeps an eye on bygone favorites and claims it has been instrumental in bringing back vintage candies that had disappeared from shelves, including nostalgic names like Bonomo's Turkish Taffy, Slo Poke, Regal Crown, and Broadway licorice rolls.

All that would be enough to lure any candy fan, but b.a. Sweetie Candy Company is much more than just a candy store. It's a bona fide family-fun destination, offering Golfland Park, which has two 18-hole mini golf courses, complete with lights for evening play, koi ponds, a cascading waterfall, and concession stands. Meanwhile, the Soda Shoppe serves up homemade ice cream, sundaes, malts, and over 100 sodas in a barn-style parlor.

This New York City treasure actually started as a shoe and hat repair shop — but a little push cart outside also sold candy. According to company lore, in the Depression years, 1937, the business owners decided to focus on their biggest moneymaker, candy, and became known as Economy Candy. After World War II, Morris "Moishe" Cohen and his brother in law assumed ownership and expanded the business, selling candy, chocolate, gift baskets, dried fruit, nuts, and more. Morris' son, Jerry, and his wife, Ilene, took over after its move to the current location at 108 Rivington Street, then passed the business to son Mitchell, who runs it today.

In other words, this living legend is a true family affair — and a multigenerational sensation that has become a part of the rich history of New York City. In 2023, the northwest corner of Rivington and Essex Streets were co-named Morris "Moishe" Cohen Way in honor of Morris and Economy Candy's lasting legacies.

Today, the store still boasts over 2,000 items for sale, and visitors routinely rave about its massive selection and reasonable prices online. Hot sellers include chocolate-covered graham crackers (with and without jelly), chocolate-covered pretzels, jelly rings, gummies, and those hard-to-find candy bars. For those outside New York City, Economy Candy offers online sales, as well.

A candy shop with old-fashioned soda fountain treats like ice cream, specialty chocolate candies and fudge, more than 400 candies for buying in bulk, and 3,000-plus wrapped candies — all in colorful circus-theme surroundings? Yes, please.

The Big Top Candy Shop has been serving the Austin community (as well as candy-minded travelers) since 2007. Visitors praised its wall-to-wall candy selection, laid out in candy-colored rows, jars, racks, and even in a lollipop tree. Passing by Peanuts, the elephant pictured on the shop's entrance (facing the city's famed South Congress Avenue, known for housing quirky boutiques), visitors will find a whimsical wonderland at Big Top Candy with classic soda machines, retro candies, and a hefty bulk section customers can grab by the scoop.

The store promises both nostalgic favorites and new creations from around the globe. Whether you're just passing through for SXSW or a stalwart resident, Big Top Candy Shop is a must-visit in the Live Music Capital of the World.

Minnesota's Largest Candy Store in Jordan, Minnesota, nods to its mind-boggling mass of inventory in its very name — and the company would seem intent on living up to that moniker. Owned by Robert Wagner, and also known as Jim's Apple Farm, the store houses not only nostalgic candy, but fresh-baked pies and strudels, the world's largest selection of sodas, an array of popcorn flavors, and locally-sourced items (think pastas, jams, jellies, and even puzzles). These are all sourced from surrounding farms, making this Midwestern gem not only a candy emporium but a true shopping destination that supports locals and promotes Minnesota products to everyone who enters.

Fortunately, its location is relatively convenient for passers-through, as the store is only 35 miles from Minneapolis. And you can't miss it — the store is housed in a massive, bright yellow barn. It's a must-stop not only thanks to its dizzying array of sweet and savory treats, but fun touches throughout its interior decor, such as a new observatory-like dome featuring a mural with more than two dozen superheroes, an animatronic band, and a fortune-telling machine. Essentially, this Minnesota behemoth will bring out the kid in anyone.

20430 Johnson Memorial Dr, Jordan, MN 55352

Calling itself one of the oldest continuously operated, family-owned candy businesses in the U.S., Schimpff's Confectionery has been hailed as America's best candy store. It was also featured on a national television special "Disney Celebrates America: The Pursuit of Happiness."

With 135 years of history, Schimpff's Confectionery more than deserves those honors — its recipes and business stretch back to the 1800s. The company history notes that the recipe for its famous Cinnamon Red Hots were handwritten in the recipe book of Gustav "Gus" Schimpff Sr. back in 1891. And it's still making waves, having been featured on several shows and publications.

With such an illustrious history, it makes sense that Schimpff's Confectionery also houses a candy museum, with thousands of pieces of American candy memorabilia. The museum, along with a candy demonstration area, were added to an adjacent building in 2001, a dream child of 1990s-era owners Warren Schimpff and his wife Jill. Today, fifth-generation owners Steve and Beth Shepherd have taken the helm and embrace the time-honored traditions and recipes at Schimpff's Confectionery.

Seeking candy from the 1970s, or maybe your favorite candy from the 1990s? The Peppermint Stick Candy Store & Ice Cream Parlor in Boyertown, Pennsylvania, stocks a cornucopia of vintage candies alongside modern-day favorites and gourmet goodies like truffles. Whether you're visiting in-store or shopping online, this candy store has got you covered. In fact, its website has a handy online shopping feature, making it easy for customers to browse by decade.

Opened in 2015, this woman-owned business also offers Longacre's ice cream for indulgent sundaes and 20-ounce milkshakes, plus bakery delights like Ice Cream Nachos (waffle cones make the chips) and the Cinnamon Roll Sundae, and a Soda Jerk menu with soda fountain favorites. Customers will find not just a store, but an unforgettable experience at The Peppermint Stick Candy Store & Ice Cream Parlor. They can find fudge, artisan chocolates, loose chocolates, gummy candy, penny candy, nostalgic candy, gourmet truffles (in flavors like mint, Champagne, tiramisu, and key lime), and even a penny candy section. Basically, if you leave hungry, you've done something wrong.

26 E Philadelphia Ave, Boyertown, PA 19512

Since 1934, Bright's Candies has been whipping up candy the old-fashioned way. Even now, this destination features charming equipment to make its treats, including large copper kettles, metal candy molds, and an antique popcorn popper in its candy kitchen. Even better, the viewing windows in the shop are designed to give everyone a front row look at the process, allowing kids and adults to watch the staff confectioners at work. All of these factors contribute to an impressively high Yelp rating, where customers called it cute and charming, with a heavenly smell and friendly staff members.

This candy store won national recognition for its sweet treats, and for decades, has been known for wafting aromas of caramel corn and waffle cones down Walla Walla's Main Street. Try out the chocolates, truffles, and seasonal items like handmade chocolate Easter bunnies. Or, go for fudge, licorice, or colorful frozen treats. In other words, it's not just a candy store; it's a place to immerse all of your senses in sweets. What's not to love about that?

This list was compiled using review sites like Reddit, Google, and Tripadvisor; research on candy stores' websites from coast to coast; and tracking media mentions on major news outlets. Extra attention was given to candy stores that are historic and/or boast unique offerings to visitors, such as mini golf, soda fountains, museums, and more.

#9693. Sola Security Brings Prof. Randall Balestriero on Board to Explore World Models for Cybersecurity

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

The next stage of enterprise cybersecurity may depend on a capability that goes beyond identifying threats: understanding how an organization's technology environment works as a connected system.

A compromised identity, for example, can create risks that extend beyond the account itself. Determining which workloads it can access, how its permissions interact with infrastructure, and what could happen if those permissions are revoked requires an understanding of relationships across an enterprise environment.

Sola Security believes this kind of contextual understanding could shape the next generation of cybersecurity agents. In a press release announcing its latest research appointment, the company said it has brought Prof. Randall Balestriero onto its scientific advisory board to advance that vision.

Balestriero is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Brown University and a visiting researcher at Meta AI Research (FAIR). He has worked alongside renowned AI researcher Yann LeCun and co-authored research with him. His work focuses on self-supervised learning and representation learning, including how AI systems develop structured representations of the world around them.

At Sola, he will advise on research directions that connect these foundational AI concepts with the everyday challenges of enterprise security.

Enterprise security environments contain interconnected identities, permissions, workloads, and infrastructure dependencies. Yet many security questions cannot be answered by examining a single suspicious event or configuration.

Identifying a compromised identity, for instance, does not automatically reveal the full extent of its access. Security teams need to understand which workloads that identity can reach and how its permissions relate to other components.

The response itself can introduce additional operational considerations. Revoking access may affect other systems or workloads, making it important to understand what could break before implementing a change.

This creates a distinction between detecting a security problem and understanding its implications.

Sola's approach centers on the idea that AI agents need a continuously updated representation of the environments they protect. Instead of processing disconnected findings, agents should be able to understand how different components relate and evaluate the potential consequences of proposed actions.

The concept of world models is central to Sola's research direction. The company sees new types of models capable of understanding environments and relationships as a potential foundation for more advanced cybersecurity agents.

Applied to enterprise security, these principles could help AI systems build comprehensive representations of organizational environments. An agent could potentially reason about how identities connect to workloads, what permissions actually enable, and how a security intervention might affect other parts of an organization.

This would change the role of an AI security agent.

Rather than simply responding to an alert, an agent with a deeper understanding of its environment could evaluate different possible actions and consider their downstream effects. The objective is to make decisions with greater awareness of operational context.

For example, an agent identifying a compromised identity would need to do more than flag the account. It would need to understand the identity's potential reach, assess the consequences of removing its access, and determine an appropriate response.

That distinction is important as enterprises increasingly introduce AI agents into security operations, where investigating threats, managing access, and carrying out remediation actions can involve interconnected systems.

Balestriero's appointment brings expertise in representation learning and self-supervised learning into Sola's research efforts.

His work examines how AI systems develop structured representations of the world around them. Sola intends to explore how perspectives from this area of foundational AI research can inform the development of security agents capable of understanding complex enterprise environments.

Guy Flechter, Co-Founder and CEO of Sola Security, believes the industry needs to rethink what it expects from security systems.

"Cybersecurity has spent years building systems that can identify problems, but understanding the environment behind those problems is an entirely different challenge," said Flechter. “We believe the next generation of security agents will need something closer to a world model: an understanding of how systems connect, how changes propagate, and what the consequences of an action will be before it is taken.”

He also emphasized the value of bringing Balestriero's research perspective into the company's work.

"Randall brings a depth of expertise in how AI systems learn representations of the world. Bringing that perspective into cybersecurity is an important step for us. We want to build agents that don't just react to what they observe, but understand the environments they protect and can reason about the impact of their decisions."

The appointment reflects Sola's position as a research-driven cybersecurity lab focused on the intersection of foundational AI research and enterprise security.

Rather than limiting innovation to adapting existing AI models for established security workflows, the company is exploring how advances in AI could enable systems to understand relationships, dependencies, and potential outcomes.

As AI agents take on more responsibilities in enterprise security, this distinction could become increasingly significant. Systems that understand the environments they operate in may be better positioned to assess risks and evaluate the consequences of their actions.

For Sola, bringing Balestriero onto its scientific advisory board is a step toward exploring that possibility.

#9691. Forget Plain Butter: Drizzle This Rich Ingredient Over Stuffing For 10x The Flavor

When it comes to the Thanksgiving feast, Americans' favorite sides include mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, and of course, stuffing. Whether it comes from a box or is lovingly homemade, stuffing is a filling, savory, and surprisingly historical part of many Turkey Day spreads. And there are seemingly as many variations of stuffing as there are households in the U.S., but butter is a unifying and necessary ingredient that no version of this Thanksgiving side can go without. However, if you really want to up the richness and flavor of your next casserole dish of stuffing, forget plain old regular butter and instead try brown butter.

Brown butter is most notably used in sweet baked goods, but the golden, nutty version can truly enhance pretty much anything where regular butter is used, including savory dishes like stuffing. What it adds to your T-giving side is a sumptuous, caramelly flavor that creates a world of depth and complexity, as the sweetness of the brown butter beautifully complements all the savory ingredients in the stuffing, like the softened bread cubes, sausage (if you use any), and the fresh herbs.

Don't skimp on it, either. If you're going to use brown butter in stuffing, you'll need to start with quite a bit of butter, perhaps as much as two to three full sticks, because the flavors in your typical stuffing can be bold, and you want to be able to taste the butterscotch-y nuttiness, which pairs so well with sage and onion, or the mushroom in a classic sausage and mushroom stuffing. Even if you make a pumpkin and herb stuffing, full of warming spices and chili, brown butter will enhance the subtle sweetness of the pumpkin and the juiciness of the raisins.

If you're inspired to try using brown butter in your stuffing this year for Thanksgiving, but you've never made it before and you're a little intimidated by it, we've a few tips to get you started. First thing, the color of the pan you use matters because you'll want to keep a close eye on how dark the butter is getting — hard to do in cast iron. The choice is yours whether you use salted or unsalted butter, but you'll want to adjust the seasonings in your stuffing accordingly. It's important that you don't use too high a heat; a good medium to medium-low will do the trick. And finally, don't walk away while your butter is browning because the process is quick, and you can go from delectably golden brown with a nutty aroma to burnt and bitter in a hurry.

There are a number of ways to incorporate brown butter into your stuffing, and whichever you choose, you'll want to remove the pan off the heat as soon as the butter is ready. You might add the veggies, aromatics, and herbs directly into the brown butter pan and let those saturate and saute in the nutty goodness, then add them to the bread element. Or you can remove the brown butter from the pan and keep it aside in a bowl, saute the vegetables, add everything into the waiting bowl of butter, and toss to combine.

#9688. Give Burgers A Protein Boost By Adding One Canned Ingredient To Ground Beef

When you need protein to help support your body after a workout or to keep you satiated throughout the day, you can reach for a number of foods, but we'd venture that there isn't a tastier option than a hamburger or cheeseburger. There are plenty of fast food options that are positively awash in the macronutrient, but cooking at home gives you far more control. Now, ground beef is obviously chock-full of protein, with anywhere from 16 to 24 grams per 4-ounce serving, but if you have a serious goal you need to meet before EOD, there is a canned ingredient that is probably lurking in your pantry (and if it isn't, it should be) that can help push you over the edge. It's beans!

Depending on the type of bean you use, a half-cup typically contains between 7 and 9 grams of protein that you can add to your meat mixture, and ultimately, black beans would be our first choice. Not only are they closest in color to a perfectly grilled burger, but they're surprisingly meaty. When they're mashed and mixed in with the ground beef, they blend right in, and their mild flavor means they take on whatever seasonings you include without drawing attention to themselves (oh, and there's the added bonus that, in addition to the extra protein, they're also a high-fiber food). By the way, if you don't have black beans on hand, you can absolutely use pinto, cannellini, or even red kidney beans.

Canned beans are often packed in a gooey liquid that consists of the starches and other substances that seep out of the beans, mixed with water and sometimes a bit of salt. As such, they are too wet straight out of the can to use in your burger mixture, so you should drain them and then dry them as much as you can (otherwise, your patties could be a soggy mess). You can even help the process by wicking as much moisture out of them as possible, making for a much more desirable texture, by placing them in a single layer on a baking sheet and popping them in the oven for a few minutes.

Mashing the beans by hand before adding them to the ground beef will always be preferable to the evisceration they'd receive in a food processor. Taking a potato masher (or you could use your meat chopper from the Dollar Tree) to the beans produces a variety of different shapes, which is useful not just for aesthetic purposes (the irregularities in the beans mimic the natural lumps that form when burger patties cook), but also for a more satisfyingly hearty bite.

Now, beans and ground beef alone do not a burger patty make; you may want to include some binders to help hold everything together. This might be as simple as an egg or two and breadcrumbs — which type of breadcrumbs is totally up to you, because typical fine-textured crumbs will work, as will panko — plus a condiment of your choice, like ketchup, mustard, or even tangy barbecue sauce.

#9685. For The Best Scrambled Eggs With Extra Fiber, Make Them Turkish Style

Getting your morning fiber doesn't have to be all about eating more fruits or specialty yogurts. Instead, you can deliciously upgrade your scrambled eggs with classic Turkish vegetables in menemen, a sort of low-effort dish that comes loaded with nutrients.

A proper menemen is customizable, but always requires three things: eggs, tomatoes, and peppers. It lets you get so much fiber because it starts with sauteing the vegetables until they soften and reduce in size, so you can load up quite a bit in a single meal. While the exact nutritional profile varies between different types of tomatoes, there's an average of about 2.16 grams of fiber per cup. The sauteing step means you can easily add two cups and cook them down to a thick, jammy consistency, providing a delicious brightness to the eggs just over 4 grams of fiber all in one go.

This is without even mentioning the fiber in the peppers. Banana peppers are relatively high in fiber, clocking in at around 4 grams per cup. Bell peppers are also quite tasty, with some varieties providing about 3 grams per cup. Since the recommended daily fiber intake for most adults hovers between 25 and 38 grams, you could potentially get a substantial portion of your daily needs all in one go. And unlike shakshuka and eggs in purgatory, two similar dishes that traditionally rely on poaching or braising, menemen lets you control the texture quite easily, whether you like your eggs creamy, fluffy, or dense.

Between the rich flavors of menemen and the plethora of foods it can pair with, you've got ample room to deliciously add even more fiber to your breakfast. Taking inspiration from a traditional Turkish breakfast is a great place to start, but don't be afraid to treat your menemen as a starting point rather than a set-in-stone recipe.

Like many countries, Turkey is a big believer in some early morning carbs, and bread products are a great way to add a bit more fiber to your diet. While a slice of white bread may be versatile and provide some sweetness to round out the tomatoes' acidity, one slice also only has about 0.6 grams of fiber. Instead, look to rye, a bread that may not be for everyone but can have three times the fiber of white bread. A slice of pumpernickel can even add 2.7 more grams of fiber to your morning, and the rich, earthy aromas and dense texture are a great contrast to creamy eggs and veggies.

Few fruits are quite so high in fiber as avocado, with a single medium-sized fruit containing around 10 grams of fiber. As a topping for menemen, its rich creaminess works perfectly with the sharper vegetable flavors, while the eggs provide plenty of protein. Half an avocado smeared over pumpernickel and topped with menemen could provide around 16 grams of fiber from all the different sources, roughly half of what many people need per day.

#9683. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!
